```nim
## Monoids: a way to combine two values, and a value that changes nothing (ADR-NCK-0002 S3, S6).
##
## A `Monoid[T]` bundles `empty` and `combine` and is only a monoid if two laws hold:
## `combine(empty, x) == x == combine(x, empty)` (identity) and
## `combine(combine(a, b), c) == combine(a, combine(b, c))` (associativity). Associativity is what
## lets `mconcat` fold a sequence in any grouping, for example in halves on two threads, and
## identity is what gives an empty input a sensible answer. `Monoid` values are built by the
## constructors below; the laws are checked by the tests, not by the type.
##
## Integer `sum` and `product` assume no overflow: with overflow they are not even defined, so they
## are not a monoid on all of `int`.

import std/tables

type
  Monoid*[T] = object
    empty*: T
    combine*: proc(a, b: T): T {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func sumMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  Monoid[int](empty: 0, combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a + b)

func productMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  Monoid[int](empty: 1, combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a * b)

func maxMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The identity is `low(int)`: the maximum of nothing is the smallest `int`.
  Monoid[int](empty: low(int), combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = max(a, b))

func minMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The identity is `high(int)`.
  Monoid[int](empty: high(int), combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = min(a, b))

func stringMonoid*(): Monoid[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Concatenation: associative but not commutative.
  Monoid[string](empty: "", combine: proc(a, b: string): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a & b)

func seqMonoid*[T](): Monoid[seq[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  Monoid[seq[T]](empty: @[], combine: proc(a, b: seq[T]): seq[T] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a & b)

func mapMonoid*[K, V](values: Monoid[V]): Monoid[Table[K, V]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Merges tables; a key present in both gets `values.combine(left, right)`. The result is a
  ## monoid whenever `values` is, and is commutative exactly when `values.combine` is.
  Monoid[Table[K, V]](
    empty: initTable[K, V](),
    combine: proc(a, b: Table[K, V]): Table[K, V] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      result = a
      for k, v in b:
        # An absent key counts as `values.empty`, which changes nothing when combined.
        result[k] = values.combine(result.getOrDefault(k, values.empty), v))

func mconcat*[T](m: Monoid[T]; xs: openArray[T]): T {.raises: [].} =
  ## Combines all the elements, left to right; an empty input gives `m.empty`.
  result = m.empty
  for x in xs:
    result = m.combine(result, x)

func foldMap*[A, T](m: Monoid[T]; xs: openArray[A];
    f: proc(x: A): T {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): T {.raises: [].} =
  ## Maps every element into the monoid and combines the results, without building the mapped list.
  result = m.empty
  for x in xs:
    result = m.combine(result, f(x))
```

```nim
## Smart constructors: parse once, then carry a type that cannot be wrong (ADR-NCK-0002 S2, S3).
##
## `Username` and `Quantity` are objects with a private field and `{.requiresInit.}`. Outside this
## module there is no way to write `Quantity(...)` or `var q: Quantity` (an unset one would hold
## 0, out of range): the only routines that build them are `parseUsername`, `parseQuantity` and
## `parseQuantityText`, and each returns a `Result`, so a caller cannot get a value without
## handling the failure. Every function that takes a `Quantity` can then rely on the range without
## checking again ("parse, don't validate"). `parseOrder` shows the railway: the first failing
## field decides the error.
##
## A plain `distinct int` is not enough for this: `distinct` stops accidental mixing with other
## types, but `Quantity(5000)` still compiles anywhere and a default value is 0. Use `distinct`
## for units and identifiers that carry no rule; use a sealed object (as here) when the type must
## guarantee a rule. Read a field of a `Result` only after checking `isOk` (or use `valueOr`):
## `.value` on an error raises `FieldDefect`.

import std/strutils
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  ParseError* = enum
    tooShort, tooLong, badCharacter, outOfRange, notANumber

  Username* {.requiresInit.} = object
    ## 3 to 16 characters from `a-z`, `0-9`, `_`; always lower case.
    raw: string
  Quantity* {.requiresInit.} = object
    ## A whole number from 1 to 1000.
    n: int

  Order* {.requiresInit.} = object
    who*: Username
    qty*: Quantity

const
  minNameLen* = 3
  maxNameLen* = 16
  minQuantity* = 1
  maxQuantity* = 1000

func `==`*(a, b: Username): bool {.raises: [].} = a.raw == b.raw
func `==`*(a, b: Quantity): bool {.raises: [].} = a.n == b.n
func `$`*(u: Username): string {.raises: [].} = u.raw
func `$`*(q: Quantity): string {.raises: [].} = $q.n

func value*(u: Username): string {.raises: [].} = u.raw
func value*(q: Quantity): int {.raises: [].} = q.n

func parseUsername*(raw: string): Result[Username, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Trims, lower-cases, then checks length and alphabet. Parsing the text of a parsed
  ## username gives the same username back.
  let s = raw.strip.toLowerAscii
  if s.len < minNameLen: return err(Username, tooShort)
  if s.len > maxNameLen: return err(Username, tooLong)
  for c in s:
    if c notin {'a'..'z', '0'..'9', '_'}:
      return err(Username, badCharacter)
  ok(Username(raw: s), ParseError)

func parseQuantity*(n: int): Result[Quantity, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Accepts exactly `minQuantity .. maxQuantity`.
  if n < minQuantity or n > maxQuantity: err(Quantity, outOfRange)
  else: ok(Quantity(n: n), ParseError)

func parseQuantityText*(raw: string): Result[Quantity, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Like `parseQuantity` for text; text that is not a whole number (or does not fit an `int`)
  ## is `notANumber`.
  var n = 0
  try:
    n = parseInt(raw.strip)
  except ValueError:
    return err(Quantity, notANumber)
  parseQuantity(n)

func plus*(a, b: Quantity): Result[Quantity, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Adds two quantities; a total above `maxQuantity` is `outOfRange`, not a wrapped value.
  parseQuantity(a.n + b.n)

func parseOrder*(who: string; qty: int): Result[Order, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The username is checked first; the quantity only if the username was fine.
  parseUsername(who).flatMap(proc(u: Username): Result[Order, ParseError] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    parseQuantity(qty).map(proc(q: Quantity): Order {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Order(who: u, qty: q)))
```

```nim
## The OO pattern groups several `createX()` methods in an interface so that a client gets
## products that belong together (all dark, all light). In Nim the family is an object whose
## fields are procs; choosing the family is choosing one value. Use it when several products must

    wkButton, wkCheckbox

    button*: MakeButton
    checkbox*: MakeCheckbox

  case t
  of themeLight: "light"
  of themeDark: "dark"

func boxMark(s: CheckState): string {.raises: [].} =
  case s
  of csChecked: "[x] "
  of csUnchecked: "[ ] "

func kitFor*(t: Theme): WidgetKit {.raises: [].} =
  ## The only place that knows which concrete products belong to which theme.
  let fam = familyTag(t)

    family: fam,
    button: proc(label: string): Widget {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Widget(family: fam, kind: wkButton, text: "[" & label & "]"),

      Widget(family: fam, kind: wkCheckbox, text: boxMark(state) & label))

  w.family & ":" & w.text

  ## Client code: sees only the kit, never a concrete theme.
  @[kit.checkbox("remember " & user, remember), kit.button("sign in")]
```

Write the Nim module `actor.nim` (Actor).

Actor: behaviour is a pure transition and effects are data (ADR-NCK-0002).

An actor is not an object with a mutable handler. Its whole behaviour is one pure function
`step(self, state, msg): Reaction` that returns the next state and a list of effects as data:
send a message to an address, spawn another actor, stop itself. "Become" (changing behaviour)
is therefore a change of the state value, never the replacement of a handler. A mailbox is a
persistent FIFO value. Nothing here delivers anything by itself: the host loop (`deliver`,
`runRounds`) takes one message from a mailbox, calls `step` and applies the effects, so the
actor can be tested without threads, timers or mocks, and a message log replays to the same
states. The `System` value in this module is a small, pure reference host (one thread, one
message at a time, round-robin); a real program replaces it with a host that performs I/O,
time and scheduling, and keeps `step` unchanged.

```nim
## Actor: behaviour is a pure transition and effects are data (ADR-NCK-0002).
##
## An actor is not an object with a mutable handler. Its whole behaviour is one pure function
## `step(self, state, msg): Reaction` that returns the next state and a list of effects as data:
## send a message to an address, spawn another actor, stop itself. "Become" (changing behaviour)
## is therefore a change of the state value, never the replacement of a handler. A mailbox is a
## persistent FIFO value. Nothing here delivers anything by itself: the host loop (`deliver`,
## `runRounds`) takes one message from a mailbox, calls `step` and applies the effects, so the
## actor can be tested without threads, timers or mocks, and a message log replays to the same
## states. The `System` value in this module is a small, pure reference host (one thread, one
## message at a time, round-robin); a real program replaces it with a host that performs I/O,
## time and scheduling, and keeps `step` unchanged.
##
## `self` is passed to `step` because an actor must be able to put its own address in a message
## (a reply-to, a greeting); it is a constant of the actor, so the transition stays a function of
## its inputs. Spawn gives the child its first message (`greeting`) and the next address; the
## parent learns the child's address because the child tells it (see the details page).

import std/options
import nimcs/ds/bankers_queue

type
  Address* = distinct int
    ## Where a message goes. The host hands them out in order, starting at 0.

  Mailbox*[M] = BankersQueue[M]
    ## A persistent FIFO: posting returns a new mailbox, the old one is unchanged.

  EffectKind* = enum
    efSend, efSpawn, efStop

  Effect*[S, M] = object
    ## A request to the host; performing it is not the actor's business.
    case kind*: EffectKind
    of efSend:
      to*: Address
      msg*: M
    of efSpawn:
      initial*: S
      greeting*: Option[M]
    of efStop:
      discard

  Reaction*[S, M] = object
    state*: S
    effects*: seq[Effect[S, M]]

  Step*[S, M] = proc(self: Address; state: S; msg: M): Reaction[S, M] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  Cell[S, M] = object
    state: S
    mailbox: Mailbox[M]
    alive: bool

  System*[S, M] = object
    ## A pure reference host: the actors (address = position), their mailboxes, the messages
    ## that could not be delivered and the number of deliveries so far.
    behaviour: Step[S, M]
    cells: seq[Cell[S, M]]
    dead: seq[(Address, M)]
    count: int

func `==`*(a, b: Address): bool {.borrow.}
func `$`*(a: Address): string {.borrow.}

func sendTo*[S, M](to: Address; msg: M): Effect[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  Effect[S, M](kind: efSend, to: to, msg: msg)

func spawnActor*[S, M](initial: S; greeting: Option[M]): Effect[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  Effect[S, M](kind: efSpawn, initial: initial, greeting: greeting)

func stopSelf*[S, M](): Effect[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  Effect[S, M](kind: efStop)

func `==`*[S, M](a, b: Effect[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of efSend: a.to == b.to and a.msg == b.msg
  of efSpawn: a.initial == b.initial and a.greeting == b.greeting
  of efStop: true

func `==`*[S, M](a, b: Reaction[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.state == b.state and a.effects == b.effects

func emptyMailbox*[M](): Mailbox[M] {.raises: [].} =
  Mailbox[M](emptyQueue[M]())

func post*[M](box: Mailbox[M]; msg: M): Mailbox[M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Appends at the back.
  Mailbox[M](BankersQueue[M](box).push(msg))

func take*[M](box: Mailbox[M]): Option[(M, Mailbox[M])] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The oldest message and the mailbox without it; `none` when empty.
  let q = BankersQueue[M](box)
  let head = q.peek
  if head.isNone: none((M, Mailbox[M]))
  else: some((head.get, Mailbox[M](q.pop)))

func pending*[M](box: Mailbox[M]): int {.raises: [].} =
  BankersQueue[M](box).len

func initSystem*[S, M](behaviour: Step[S, M]): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  System[S, M](behaviour: behaviour, cells: @[], dead: @[], count: 0)

func known[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): bool =
  int(a) >= 0 and int(a) < sys.cells.len

func addActor*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; initial: S): (System[S, M], Address) {.raises: [].} =
  ## Adds an actor with an empty mailbox; its address is the number of actors so far.
  var next = sys
  next.cells.add Cell[S, M](state: initial, mailbox: emptyMailbox[M](), alive: true)
  (next, Address(sys.cells.len))

func actorCount*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): int {.raises: [].} = sys.cells.len

func delivered*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## How many messages the host has handed to an actor.
  sys.count

func isAlive*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): bool {.raises: [].} =
  sys.known(a) and sys.cells[int(a)].alive

func stateOf*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): Option[S] {.raises: [].} =
  if sys.known(a): some(sys.cells[int(a)].state) else: none(S)

func mailboxLen*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): int {.raises: [].} =
  if sys.known(a): sys.cells[int(a)].mailbox.pending else: 0

func deadLetters*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): seq[(Address, M)] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Messages sent to an unknown or stopped actor, in the order they were refused.
  sys.dead

func isIdle*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## No live actor has a message waiting.
  for c in sys.cells:
    if c.alive and c.mailbox.pending > 0: return false
  true

func tell*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; to: Address; msg: M): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Puts `msg` in the mailbox of `to`; a message to an unknown or stopped actor is a dead letter.
  result = sys
  if sys.isAlive(to):
    result.cells[int(to)].mailbox = result.cells[int(to)].mailbox.post(msg)
  else:
    result.dead.add (to, msg)

func apply[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; self: Address; fx: Effect[S, M]): System[S, M] =
  case fx.kind
  of efSend:
    result = sys.tell(fx.to, fx.msg)
  of efSpawn:
    let (grown, child) = sys.addActor(fx.initial)
    result = grown
    if fx.greeting.isSome: result = grown.tell(child, fx.greeting.get)
  of efStop:
    result = sys
    var box = result.cells[int(self)].mailbox
    while true:
      let t = box.take
      if t.isNone: break
      result.dead.add (self, t.get[0])
      box = t.get[1]
    result.cells[int(self)].mailbox = emptyMailbox[M]()
    result.cells[int(self)].alive = false

func deliver*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The host's one move: take the oldest message of `a`, call `step`, store the new state and
  ## apply the effects in order. Nothing happens if `a` is unknown, stopped or has no message.
  if not sys.isAlive(a): return sys
  let t = sys.cells[int(a)].mailbox.take
  if t.isNone: return sys
  let (msg, rest) = t.get
  let reaction = sys.behaviour(a, sys.cells[int(a)].state, msg)
  result = sys
  result.cells[int(a)].mailbox = rest
  result.cells[int(a)].state = reaction.state
  inc result.count
  for fx in reaction.effects:
    result = result.apply(a, fx)

func runRounds*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; budget: int): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Round-robin: each round offers every actor, in address order, one delivery. Stops when the
  ## system is idle or after `budget` deliveries, whichever comes first, so a loop of actors that
  ## message each other forever cannot hang the host.
  result = sys
  let stopAt = sys.count + max(budget, 0)
  while result.count < stopAt and not result.isIdle:
    var a = 0
    while a < result.cells.len and result.count < stopAt:
      result = result.deliver(Address(a))
      inc a

func `==`*[S, M](a, b: System[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Same actors, states, mailboxes, dead letters and delivery count; the behaviour proc is not
  ## compared.
  if a.cells.len != b.cells.len or a.count != b.count or a.dead != b.dead: return false
  for i in 0 ..< a.cells.len:
    let x = a.cells[i]
    let y = b.cells[i]
    if x.alive != y.alive or x.state != y.state: return false
    if BankersQueue[M](x.mailbox).toSeq != BankersQueue[M](y.mailbox).toSeq: return false
  true
```

Write the Nim module `anti_corruption_layer.nim` (Anti-corruption layer).

Anti-corruption layer: translate a foreign model at the border so it never leaks inward.

Another system's model (a supplier's order message) has its own words, codes and number formats,
and it changes when they decide. If its types reach into your code, every change of theirs is a
change of yours, and its mistakes (a status code you never meant to support) become your states.
The layer is the only place that knows both. It is a pair of functions per foreign version: one
from the foreign record to your `Order`, built through the same smart constructor as every
order of your own, and one back; your code takes `Order` and cannot be handed a foreign record
(the compiler refuses it). A new foreign version is a new pair, and nothing inward moves.
Refusals are values with a reason and a position, not zeros and defaults. Use it where a model
you do not control meets one you do; do not use it between two parts of your own model.

Branch by abstraction: replace an implementation inside the trunk, behind an interface, in small steps.

A long-lived branch for a replacement drifts from the trunk until nobody can merge it. Branch by

```nim
## Branch by abstraction: replace an implementation inside the trunk, behind an interface, in small steps.
##
## A long-lived branch for a replacement drifts from the trunk until nobody can merge it. Branch by
## abstraction keeps one trunk: first the callers are moved behind an abstraction (here a record of
## procs, `Pricing`) that the old implementation fills, then the new implementation is written
## behind the same abstraction, then a stage value says which one answers: old, shadow (the old
## answers while both run and a mismatch is reported) or new. Callers never change when the stage
## does. The stage is a plain value moved by `advance` and `retreat`, so going forward, going
## back and "the old one is no longer consulted" are functions with laws. Use it for a replacement
## that cannot land in one commit and has no seam at the network edge (that is the strangler fig);
## remove the abstraction's losing side when the stage reaches `stNew` for good.

import std/options

type
  Stage* = enum
    stOld, stShadow, stNew

  Pricing* = object
    ## The abstraction. Contract: the sum of the line amounts in cents, a negative line counting as 0.
    subtotal*: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  Mismatch* = object
    oldTotal*, newTotal*: int

  Answer* = tuple[total: int, mismatch: Option[Mismatch]]

func oldPricing*(): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  Pricing(subtotal: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    var sum = 0
    for c in cents:
      if c > 0: sum += c
    sum)

func newPricing*(): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  ## The replacement: the same contract, written another way.
  Pricing(subtotal: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    var sum = 0
    for c in cents:
      sum += max(c, 0)
    sum)

func uncheckedPricing*(): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  ## A replacement that forgot the clamp; the shadow stage exists to find this before users do.
  Pricing(subtotal: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    var sum = 0
    for c in cents:
      sum += c
    sum)

func invoiceTotal*(p: Pricing; cents: seq[int]; taxPercent: int): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## A caller. It knows the abstraction and nothing about which implementation fills it.
  let sub = p.subtotal(cents)
  sub + sub * taxPercent div 100

func select*(stage: Stage; old, replacement: Pricing): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  ## Only `stNew` consults the replacement for the answer; the shadow stage answers with the old.
  case stage
  of stOld, stShadow: old
  of stNew: replacement

func compare*(old, replacement: Pricing; cents: seq[int]): Option[Mismatch] {.raises: [].} =
  let (a, b) = (old.subtotal(cents), replacement.subtotal(cents))
  if a == b: none(Mismatch) else: some(Mismatch(oldTotal: a, newTotal: b))

func invoiceAt*(stage: Stage; old, replacement: Pricing; cents: seq[int]; taxPercent: int): Answer {.raises: [].} =
  ## The answer at a stage; the mismatch is looked for only while the stage is `stShadow`.
  let mismatch = if stage == stShadow: compare(old, replacement, cents) else: none(Mismatch)
  (total: invoiceTotal(select(stage, old, replacement), cents, taxPercent), mismatch: mismatch)

func advance*(s: Stage): Stage {.raises: [].} =
  case s
  of stOld: stShadow
  of stShadow, stNew: stNew

func retreat*(s: Stage): Stage {.raises: [].} =
  case s
  of stOld, stShadow: stOld
  of stNew: stShadow
```

```nim
## Bridge: shapes (abstraction) and backends (implementation) vary separately.
##
## The OO pattern splits a hierarchy in two so that N shapes and M backends need N + M definitions,
## not N * M. That only works if the implementation side offers a small, *fixed* set of primitives
## that every abstraction lowers to. Here the only primitive is `line`: a `Backend` is an object
## with one proc field, a `Shape` lowers itself to line `Segment`s (`lower`), and `draw` feeds them
## to the backend. A new shape needs only a `lower` case; a new backend needs only a `line` proc;
## neither touches the other. (If the backend had one primitive per shape kind, adding a shape
## would edit every backend and this would not be a bridge.) Use it when two axes would multiply.
## Circles are approximated by an octagon with integer coordinates.

type
  Point* = object
    x*, y*: int

  Segment* = object
    a*, b*: Point

  Backend* = object
    name*: string
    line*: proc(a, b: Point): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  ShapeKind* = enum
    skRect, skCircle

  Shape* = object
    case kind*: ShapeKind
    of skRect:
      x*, y*, w*, h*: int
    of skCircle:
      cx*, cy*, r*: int

func pt(x, y: int): Point {.raises: [].} =
  Point(x: x, y: y)

func lower*(s: Shape): seq[Segment] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The shape's closed outline as line segments, independent of any backend.
  var corners: seq[Point] = @[]
  case s.kind
  of skRect:
    corners = @[pt(s.x, s.y), pt(s.x + s.w, s.y), pt(s.x + s.w, s.y + s.h), pt(s.x, s.y + s.h)]
  of skCircle:
    let d = s.r * 7 div 10 # r * cos 45 degrees, rounded down
    corners = @[pt(s.cx + s.r, s.cy), pt(s.cx + d, s.cy + d), pt(s.cx, s.cy + s.r),
                pt(s.cx - d, s.cy + d), pt(s.cx - s.r, s.cy), pt(s.cx - d, s.cy - d),
                pt(s.cx, s.cy - s.r), pt(s.cx + d, s.cy - d)]
  for i in 0 ..< corners.len:
    result.add(Segment(a: corners[i], b: corners[(i + 1) mod corners.len]))

func svgBackend*(): Backend {.raises: [].} =
  Backend(
    name: "svg",
    line: proc(a, b: Point): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      "<line x1=" & $a.x & " y1=" & $a.y & " x2=" & $b.x & " y2=" & $b.y & "/>")

func asciiBackend*(): Backend {.raises: [].} =
  Backend(
    name: "ascii",
    line: proc(a, b: Point): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      "LINE " & $a.x & "," & $a.y & " " & $b.x & "," & $b.y)

func draw*(s: Shape; b: Backend): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
```

```nim
##
## The OO pattern collects many optional settings step by step and creates the object only when it
## is complete. In Nim each `withX` returns a changed copy (the old builder stays valid), and
## `build` is the single place that checks the whole configuration and returns a `Result`.

import nimcs/fp/result

type
  Port* = distinct int

  BuildError* = enum
    beEmptyHost, beBadPort, beTlsNeedsCert, beNoWorkers

    host*: string
    port*: Port
    tls*: bool
    certPath*: Option[string]
    workers*: int

    host: string
    port: int
    tls: bool
    certPath: Option[string]
    workers: int

func `==`*(a, b: Port): bool {.borrow.}

func initConfigBuilder*(): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  ConfigBuilder(host: "", port: 8080, tls: false, certPath: none(string), workers: 1)

func withHost*(b: ConfigBuilder; host: string): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.host = host

func withPort*(b: ConfigBuilder; port: int): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.port = port

func withTls*(b: ConfigBuilder; certPath: string): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.tls = true
  result.certPath = if certPath.len > 0: some(certPath) else: none(string)

func withWorkers*(b: ConfigBuilder; workers: int): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.workers = workers

func build*(b: ConfigBuilder): Result[ServerConfig, BuildError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Checks in a fixed order, so the reported error is deterministic.
  if b.host.len == 0:
    err(ServerConfig, beEmptyHost)
  elif b.port < 1 or b.port > 65535:
    err(ServerConfig, beBadPort)
  elif b.tls and b.certPath.isNone:
    err(ServerConfig, beTlsNeedsCert)
  elif b.workers < 1:
    err(ServerConfig, beNoWorkers)
```

Write the Nim module `caretaker.nim` (Caretaker).

Caretaker: revocable forwarding, with the revocation state threaded as data (ADR-NCK-0002).

A caretaker hands out a `Forwarder` (the capability the client holds: it forwards operations to
the target) and a `Revoker` (the capability the grantor keeps: it cuts the forwarder off).
Classic caretakers use a mutable cell that every forwarder reads. Here the cell is a value:
the `Caretaker` holds one slot per forwarder, `forward` takes the caretaker as an argument and
answers `crRevoked` once the slot is empty, and `revoke` returns a new caretaker whose slot has
dropped the target. Nothing is hidden or mutable, so every law is checkable as a function of
values. The price is explicit and deliberate: revocation reaches only the callers that use the
caretaker value that was revoked. Keep the caretaker in the one place that owns the resource
(an actor's state, a store threaded through the program), and let clients call through that
owner (send it a message, or pass the current value). If independent parties must see a
revocation instantly without going through an owner, a shared mutable cell (a `ref` read by
all forwarders) is the right tool; it gives up the value semantics and the replayability of
these laws, so use it only at that edge.

`forward` runs a pure operation (`proc` with `noSideEffect`) on the target; to forward an
effectful call, return a description of the call as the result and perform it in the shell.
Every caretaker has a `brand`; its forwarders and revokers carry it, so capabilities of another
caretaker are refused (`crForeign`) instead of acting on a slot of the same number. Use one
distinct brand per caretaker.

```nim
##
## A caretaker hands out a `Forwarder` (the capability the client holds: it forwards operations to
## the target) and a `Revoker` (the capability the grantor keeps: it cuts the forwarder off).
## Classic caretakers use a mutable cell that every forwarder reads. Here the cell is a value:
## the `Caretaker` holds one slot per forwarder, `forward` takes the caretaker as an argument and
## answers `crRevoked` once the slot is empty, and `revoke` returns a new caretaker whose slot has
## dropped the target. Nothing is hidden or mutable, so every law is checkable as a function of
## values. The price is explicit and deliberate: revocation reaches only the callers that use the
## caretaker value that was revoked. Keep the caretaker in the one place that owns the resource
## (an actor's state, a store threaded through the program), and let clients call through that
## owner (send it a message, or pass the current value). If independent parties must see a
## revocation instantly without going through an owner, a shared mutable cell (a `ref` read by
## all forwarders) is the right tool; it gives up the value semantics and the replayability of
## these laws, so use it only at that edge.
##
## `forward` runs a pure operation (`proc` with `noSideEffect`) on the target; to forward an
## effectful call, return a description of the call as the result and perform it in the shell.
## Every caretaker has a `brand`; its forwarders and revokers carry it, so capabilities of another
## caretaker are refused (`crForeign`) instead of acting on a slot of the same number. Use one
## distinct brand per caretaker.

import std/options
import nimcs/ds/hamt
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  CaretakerError* = enum
    crRevoked, crForeign

  Forwarder* {.requiresInit.} = object
    brand: int
    slot: int

  Revoker* {.requiresInit.} = object
    brand: int
    slot: int

  Caretaker*[T] = object
    brand: int
    next: int
    slots: Hamt[int, Option[T]]   ## `none` once revoked: the target is no longer referenced

  Wrapped*[T] = object
    caretaker*: Caretaker[T]
    forwarder*: Forwarder
    revoker*: Revoker

func initCaretaker*[T](brand: int): Caretaker[T] {.raises: [].} =
  Caretaker[T](brand: brand, next: 0, slots: emptyHamt[int, Option[T]]())

func wrap*[T](c: Caretaker[T]; target: T): Wrapped[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A new forwarder to `target` and the revoker for it. Wrapping the same target twice gives two
  ## independent forwarders.
  Wrapped[T](
    caretaker: Caretaker[T](brand: c.brand, next: c.next + 1,
      slots: c.slots.put(c.next, some(target))),
    forwarder: Forwarder(brand: c.brand, slot: c.next),
    revoker: Revoker(brand: c.brand, slot: c.next))

func forward*[T, R](c: Caretaker[T]; f: Forwarder;
    op: proc(t: T): R {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Result[R, CaretakerError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `ok(op(target))` while the forwarder is live; `err(crRevoked)` after revocation; `err(crForeign)`
  ## for a forwarder that belongs to another caretaker.
  if f.brand != c.brand: return err(R, crForeign)
  let slot = c.slots.get(f.slot)
  if slot.isNone: return err(R, crForeign)
  if slot.get.isNone: err(R, crRevoked)
  else: ok(op(slot.get.get), CaretakerError)

func revoke*[T](c: Caretaker[T]; r: Revoker): Result[Caretaker[T], CaretakerError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Cuts off the forwarder this revoker belongs to. Revoking again changes nothing (it is `ok` of
  ## an equivalent caretaker). A revoker of another caretaker is `err(crForeign)`: it is refused,
  ## not ignored.
  if r.brand != c.brand or not c.slots.contains(r.slot): err(Caretaker[T], crForeign)
  else:
    ok(Caretaker[T](brand: c.brand, next: c.next, slots: c.slots.put(r.slot, none(T))),
      CaretakerError)

func isRevoked*[T](c: Caretaker[T]; f: Forwarder): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## True when `f` is one of this caretaker's forwarders and has been revoked.
  if f.brand != c.brand: return false
  let slot = c.slots.get(f.slot)
  slot.isSome and slot.get.isNone

func liveCount*[T](c: Caretaker[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## The forwarders that still reach their target.
  for (_, slot) in c.slots.toSortedSeq:
    if slot.isSome: inc result
```

```nim
## Composite as a recursive object variant plus a fold.
##
## The OO pattern lets clients treat a single object and a group of objects through one interface.
## In Nim the tree is one object variant (`File` or `Dir` holding a `seq` of children, no `ref`
## needed) and every operation on the whole tree is an instance of one `fold`. Use it for
## part-whole structures (file trees, UI trees, expressions); write new operations as folds
## instead of adding a method to every node kind.

type
  EntryKind* = enum
    ekFile, ekDir

  Entry* = object
    name*: string
    case kind*: EntryKind
    of ekFile:
      size*: int
    of ekDir:
      children*: seq[Entry]

func file*(name: string; size: int): Entry {.raises: [].} =
  Entry(name: name, kind: ekFile, size: size)

func dir*(name: string; children: seq[Entry]): Entry {.raises: [].} =
  Entry(name: name, kind: ekDir, children: children)

func fold*[A](e: Entry;
              onFile: proc(name: string; size: int): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].};
              onDir: proc(name: string; parts: seq[A]): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): A {.raises: [].} =
  ## The one recursion; every other operation below is a choice of `onFile` and `onDir`.
  case e.kind
  of ekFile:
    onFile(e.name, e.size)
  of ekDir:
    var parts: seq[A] = @[]
    for c in e.children:
      parts.add(fold(c, onFile, onDir))
    onDir(e.name, parts)

func totalSize*(e: Entry): int {.raises: [].} =
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = size,
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var sum = 0
      for p in parts: sum += p
      sum)

func fileCount*(e: Entry): int {.raises: [].} =
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = 1,
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var sum = 0
      for p in parts: sum += p
      sum)

func depth*(e: Entry): int {.raises: [].} =
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = 0,
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var deepest = 0
      for p in parts:
        if p > deepest: deepest = p
      deepest + 1)

func leafSizes*(e: Entry): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sizes of all files, left to right.
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): seq[int] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = @[size],
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[seq[int]]): seq[int] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var all: seq[int] = @[]
      for p in parts: all.add(p)
      all)
```

Write the Nim module `cqrs.nim` (CQRS (command query responsibility segregation)).

CQRS: commands are decided into events on one side, read models are folds of the same events on the other.

Command and query responsibility segregation splits a system in two. The write side takes a
command, checks it against the current state and answers with events or a reason for refusing;
it keeps only the state needed to decide. The read side never decides anything: each read model
is a projection, a fold over the events, shaped for the question it answers. Here both sides
consume the same event log (CQRS does not require event sourcing; the log is what makes the
projections easy to state), so read models can be added or rebuilt at will. The example is a
small warehouse: receive and ship units, with a stock table (write side) and a dashboard
(read side).

```nim
## CQRS: commands are decided into events on one side, read models are folds of the same events on the other.
##
## Command and query responsibility segregation splits a system in two. The write side takes a
## command, checks it against the current state and answers with events or a reason for refusing;
## it keeps only the state needed to decide. The read side never decides anything: each read model
## is a projection, a fold over the events, shaped for the question it answers. Here both sides
## consume the same event log (CQRS does not require event sourcing; the log is what makes the
## projections easy to state), so read models can be added or rebuilt at will. The example is a
## small warehouse: receive and ship units, with a stock table (write side) and a dashboard
## (read side).

import std/algorithm
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  StockLine* = object
    sku*: string
    qty*: int

  Stock* = object
    ## Write-side state: one line per sku that is on hand, sorted by sku, never a zero line.
    lines*: seq[StockLine]

  CommandKind* = enum
    ckReceive, ckShip

  Command* = object
    kind*: CommandKind
    sku*: string
    qty*: int

  EventKind* = enum
    evReceived, evShipped

  Event* = object
    kind*: EventKind
    sku*: string
    qty*: int

  CommandError* = enum
    ceNonPositiveQty, ceEmptySku, ceInsufficientStock

  Session* = object
    ## The application service state: current stock, the event log, and the refusals.
    stock*: Stock
    events*: seq[Event]
    rejected*: seq[CommandError]

  Dashboard* = object
    ## A read model: totals only, no per-sku detail.
    received*: int
    shipped*: int
    shipments*: int

# ── write side ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

func initStock*(): Stock {.raises: [].} = Stock(lines: @[])

func qtyOf*(stock: Stock; sku: string): int {.raises: [].} =
  for l in stock.lines:
    if l.sku == sku: return l.qty
  0

func evolve*(stock: Stock; e: Event): Stock {.raises: [].} =
  ## Applies a fact to the stock. Lines whose quantity becomes zero disappear, so equal stocks
  ## are equal values. An event that `decide` never produced (shipping more than is on hand)
  ## would leave a negative line; the guard against that lives in `decide`, not here.
  let delta = if e.kind == evReceived: e.qty else: -e.qty
  var lines: seq[StockLine]
  var seen = false
  for l in stock.lines:
    if l.sku == e.sku:
      seen = true
      if l.qty + delta != 0: lines.add StockLine(sku: l.sku, qty: l.qty + delta)
    else:
      lines.add l
  if not seen and delta != 0: lines.add StockLine(sku: e.sku, qty: delta)
  lines.sort(proc(a, b: StockLine): int = cmp(a.sku, b.sku))
  Stock(lines: lines)

func decide*(stock: Stock; cmd: Command): Result[seq[Event], CommandError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Validates a command against the stock. It returns the events that record what happens, or
  ## the first reason it must be refused; it changes nothing.
  if cmd.sku.len == 0:
    return err(seq[Event], ceEmptySku)
  if cmd.qty <= 0:
    return err(seq[Event], ceNonPositiveQty)
  case cmd.kind
  of ckReceive:
    ok(@[Event(kind: evReceived, sku: cmd.sku, qty: cmd.qty)], CommandError)
  of ckShip:
    if stock.qtyOf(cmd.sku) < cmd.qty:
      err(seq[Event], ceInsufficientStock)
    else:
      ok(@[Event(kind: evShipped, sku: cmd.sku, qty: cmd.qty)], CommandError)

func initSession*(): Session {.raises: [].} =
```

```nim
## Decorator as a function from handler to handler.
##
## The OO pattern adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same
## interface. In Nim a handler is a proc value `Request -> Response` and a decorator is
## `proc(h: Handler): Handler`; stacking decorators is function composition. Use it for
## cross-cutting behaviour (headers, authorisation, tracing) around a core handler without
## changing the core. The pipeline is pure: there is no I/O, the "log" is a trace in the response.

type
  Request* = object
    path*: string
    token*: string

  Response* = object
    status*: int
    body*: string
    trace*: seq[string]

  Handler* = proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
  Decorator* = proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func identityDecorator*(): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = h

func withTrace*(label: string): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## Records `label` before the inner handler runs and again, as `label/done`, after it returns.
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var res = h(r)
      res.trace = @[label] & res.trace & @[label & "/done"]
      res

func withAuth*(expected: string): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## Short-circuits with 401 when the token differs; the inner handler is not called.
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      if r.token == expected:
        h(r)
      else:
        Response(status: 401, body: "unauthorized", trace: @[])

func withBodySuffix*(suffix: string): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var res = h(r)
      res.body.add(suffix)
      res

func compose*(outer, inner: Decorator): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## `compose(a, b)(h)` is `a(b(h))`: `a` is the outermost wrapper and sees the request first.
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    outer(inner(h))

func stack*(ds: seq[Decorator]): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## The first element is the outermost decorator.
  var acc = identityDecorator()
  for i in countdown(ds.high, 0):
    acc = compose(ds[i], acc)
  acc
```

```nim
## Dependency record: dependencies are an object of procs, and a test double is another object.
##
## Business logic that needs the clock and a mail sender takes a `Deps` value instead of calling
## them. The production record holds the real procs; a test builds a record from a fixed clock
## and a sender that writes into a list. No interface type, no framework, no global to reset.

## dependency it cares about. Use it for the few effects a unit needs. When the sequence of
## effects itself must be inspected or optimised, make the program data instead
## (`free_interpreter`).

type
  Clock* = proc(): int {.raises: [].}
    ## Today as a day number.

  Sender* = proc(to, body: string): Result[int, string] {.raises: [].}
    ## Sends one message; the `int` is the message id, the error says why it failed.

  Deps* = object
    now*: Clock
    send*: Sender

  RemindError* = object
    ## Why a run stopped, and what had already gone out before it did.
    reason*: string
    sentIds*: seq[int]

  Invoice* = object
    id*: int
    customer*: string
    dueDay*: int
    paid*: bool

func withClock*(deps: Deps; now: Clock): Deps {.raises: [].} =
  ## The same dependencies with another clock.
  Deps(now: now, send: deps.send)

func withSender*(deps: Deps; send: Sender): Deps {.raises: [].} =
  ## The same dependencies with another sender.
  Deps(now: deps.now, send: send)

proc remindOverdue*(deps: Deps; invoices: openArray[Invoice]): Result[seq[int], RemindError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sends one reminder per unpaid invoice that is due before today, in list order, and returns
  ## the message ids. It is a `proc`, not a `func`, because the record it is given may perform
  ## effects. The first send that fails stops the run; the error carries the sender's reason and the ids
  ## of the messages already sent, which cannot be taken back.
  let today = deps.now()
  var ids: seq[int]
  for inv in invoices:
    if not inv.paid and inv.dueDay < today:
      let sent = deps.send(inv.customer, "Invoice " & $inv.id & " was due on day " & $inv.dueDay)
      if sent.isErr:
        return err(seq[int], RemindError(reason: sent.error, sentIds: ids))
      ids.add sent.value
  ok(ids, RemindError)
```

```nim
## Event sourcing: the state of an entity is a fold over the facts that happened to it.
##
## Instead of storing the current balance, store the list of events (deposited, withdrawn) and
## compute the balance by folding `apply` over them. The log is the source of truth and is only
## ever appended to; any past state can be rebuilt, and a snapshot is nothing but a saved
## intermediate value of the same fold. Use it when the history matters (audit, undo, temporal
## queries) or when several read models must be derived from the same facts (see `cqrs`).

type
  EventKind* = enum
    evDeposited, evWithdrawn

  Event* = object
    ## A fact in the past tense. `amount` is positive; the direction is in `kind`.
    kind*: EventKind
    amount*: int

  Account* = object
    ## The folded state. `version` counts the events folded in.
    balance*: int
    version*: int

func deposited*(amount: Positive): Event {.raises: [].} =
  Event(kind: evDeposited, amount: amount)

func withdrawn*(amount: Positive): Event {.raises: [].} =
  Event(kind: evWithdrawn, amount: amount)

func initAccount*(): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## The state before any event: the fold's starting value.
  Account(balance: 0, version: 0)

func apply*(a: Account; e: Event): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## One step of the fold. Total: events are facts, so it never refuses one (a command that
  ## would overdraw is refused before an event exists, see `cqrs`).
  let delta =
    case e.kind
    of evDeposited: e.amount
    of evWithdrawn: -e.amount
  Account(balance: a.balance + delta, version: a.version + 1)

func replayFrom*(snapshot: Account; tail: openArray[Event]): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## Continues the fold from a saved state.
  result = snapshot
  for e in tail:
    result = result.apply(e)

func replay*(events: openArray[Event]): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## The whole fold from the empty account.
  initAccount().replayFrom(events)

func snapshotAt*(events: openArray[Event]; upTo: int): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## The state after the first `upTo` events; a count below 0 or beyond the log is clamped.
  let n = max(0, min(upTo, events.len))
  replay(events.toOpenArray(0, n - 1))

func appended*(log: seq[Event]; e: Event): seq[Event] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A new log with `e` at the end; `log` itself is untouched.
  result = log
  result.add e
```

```nim
## Flyweight as interning against an explicit immutable pool value.
##
## The OO pattern shares one object among many users when the objects are identical, to save memory
## and to make equality a cheap comparison. In Nim the shared thing is a `Sym` (an index) and the
## pool is a value you pass in and get back: `intern` returns the new pool and the symbol. No
## global table, so interning is deterministic and testable. `intern` copies the pool when it adds a
## string (O(pool)); to intern many strings use `internAll`, which copies once. Use it for many repeated strings
## (identifiers, font names, tags); skip it when the data is small or unique.

import std/[options, tables]

type
  Sym* = distinct int

  Pool* = object
    names: seq[string]
    index: Table[string, int]

func `==`*(a, b: Sym): bool {.borrow.}

func `==`*(a, b: Pool): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Pools are equal when they hold the same strings in the same order (`index` is derived).
  a.names == b.names

func initPool*(): Pool {.raises: [].} =
  Pool(names: @[], index: initTable[string, int]())

func size*(p: Pool): int {.raises: [].} =
  p.names.len

func intern*(p: Pool; s: string): tuple[pool: Pool, sym: Sym] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Symbols are numbered by first appearance. Interning a string the pool already holds returns
  ## the same pool and the same symbol (idempotent).
  if p.index.hasKey(s):
    (p, Sym(p.index.getOrDefault(s, 0)))
  else:
    var next = p
    let id = next.names.len
    next.names.add(s)
    next.index[s] = id
    (next, Sym(id))

func resolve*(p: Pool; sym: Sym): Option[string] {.raises: [].} =
  let i = int(sym)
  if i >= 0 and i < p.names.len: some(p.names[i]) else: none(string)

func internAll*(p: Pool; items: seq[string]): tuple[pool: Pool, syms: seq[Sym]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Same result as interning one by one, but the pool is copied once, not once per new string.
  var next = p
  var syms: seq[Sym] = @[]
  for s in items:
    let known = next.index.getOrDefault(s, -1)
    if known >= 0:
      syms.add(Sym(known))
    else:
      let id = next.names.len
      next.names.add(s)
      next.index[s] = id
      syms.add(Sym(id))
  (next, syms)
```

```nim
##
## Instead of calling a key-value store directly, build a `Program`, a list of instruction
## values (`put`, `get`, `delete`, `whenMissing`). Nothing happens while building. Then hand the
## program to an interpreter: `runPure` folds it over an in-memory store, `pretty` prints it,
## a real interpreter could talk to a database. This is dependency injection by interpreter, and
## because the program is data it can also be rewritten (`simplify`) before it runs, which a
## closure cannot be. Use it when you want to test, inspect or optimise the sequence of effects
## without performing them. When programs are fixed and only the backend varies, a record of
## procs (`dependency_record`) is lighter; for new interpreters without a data type see
## `tagless_final`.

import std/[algorithm, options]

type
  InstrKind* = enum
    ikPut, ikGet, ikDelete, ikWhenMissing

  Instr* = object
    case kind*: InstrKind
    of ikPut:
      putKey*, putValue*: string
    of ikGet, ikDelete:
      key*: string
    of ikWhenMissing:
      missingKey*: string
      body*: seq[Instr]   ## runs only when `missingKey` has no value

  Program* = seq[Instr]

  Entry* = object
    key*, value*: string

  Outcome* = object
    ## What the pure interpreter produces: the final store (sorted by key) and the lines `get`
    ## printed, `key=value` or `key=<missing>`.
    store*: seq[Entry]
    output*: seq[string]

func `==`*(a, b: Instr): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of ikPut: a.putKey == b.putKey and a.putValue == b.putValue
  of ikGet, ikDelete: a.key == b.key
  of ikWhenMissing: a.missingKey == b.missingKey and a.body == b.body

func put*(key, value: string): Instr {.raises: [].} =
  Instr(kind: ikPut, putKey: key, putValue: value)

func get*(key: string): Instr {.raises: [].} = Instr(kind: ikGet, key: key)

func del*(key: string): Instr {.raises: [].} = Instr(kind: ikDelete, key: key)

func whenMissing*(key: string; body: Program): Instr {.raises: [].} =
  Instr(kind: ikWhenMissing, missingKey: key, body: body)

func ensureDefault*(key, value: string): Program {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sets `key` only if it has no value. Running it twice equals running it once.
  @[whenMissing(key, @[put(key, value)])]

# ── interpreter 1: pure ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

func lookup(store: seq[Entry]; key: string): Option[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for e in store:
    if e.key == key: return some(e.value)
  none(string)

func upsert(store: seq[Entry]; key, value: string): seq[Entry] {.raises: [].} =
  var found = false
  for e in store:
    if e.key == key:
      found = true
      result.add Entry(key: key, value: value)
    else:
      result.add e
  if not found:
    result.add Entry(key: key, value: value)
    result.sort(proc(a, b: Entry): int = cmp(a.key, b.key))

func remove(store: seq[Entry]; key: string): seq[Entry] {.raises: [].} =
  for e in store:
    if e.key != key: result.add e

func exec(state: Outcome; p: openArray[Instr]): Outcome {.raises: [].} =
  result = state
  for i in p:
    case i.kind
    of ikPut:
      result.store = result.store.upsert(i.putKey, i.putValue)
    of ikGet:
      let found = result.store.lookup(i.key)
      result.output.add i.key & "=" & (if found.isSome: found.get else: "<missing>")
    of ikDelete:
      result.store = result.store.remove(i.key)
    of ikWhenMissing:
      if result.store.lookup(i.missingKey).isNone:
        result = exec(result, i.body)

func runPure*(p: Program; start: seq[Entry] = @[]): Outcome {.raises: [].} =
  ## Interprets `p` over `start` (a store as `runPure` itself returns it, sorted by key).
  exec(Outcome(store: start, output: @[]), p)

# ── interpreter 2: printer ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

func prettyLines(p: openArray[Instr]; indent: string): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for i in p:
    case i.kind
    of ikPut: result.add indent & "put " & i.putKey & " = " & i.putValue
    of ikGet: result.add indent & "get " & i.key
    of ikDelete: result.add indent & "delete " & i.key
    of ikWhenMissing:
      result.add indent & "when-missing " & i.missingKey
      result.add prettyLines(i.body, indent & "  ")

func pretty*(p: Program): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## One line per instruction, bodies indented by two spaces; an empty program prints as "".
  let lines = prettyLines(p, "")
  for n, line in lines:
    if n > 0: result.add "\n"
    result.add line

func `$`*(i: Instr): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The instruction as `pretty` prints it.
  pretty(@[i])

func size*(p: Program): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Number of instructions, bodies included.
  for i in p:
    result += 1
    if i.kind == ikWhenMissing: result += size(i.body)

# ── a program-to-program rewrite ───────────────────────────────────────────

func isWrite(i: Instr): bool {.raises: [].} = i.kind in {ikPut, ikDelete}

func writtenKey(i: Instr): string {.raises: [].} =
  if i.kind == ikPut: i.putKey else: i.key

func simplify*(p: Program): Program {.raises: [].} =
  ## Drops a `put` or `delete` that the next instruction overwrites with another `put` or
  ## `delete` of the same key (nothing could read it in between), inside bodies too. The result
  ## runs to the same store and output (PAT-FREEINTERPRETER-04) and simplifying again changes
  ## nothing.
  for instr in p:
    var cur = instr
    if cur.kind == ikWhenMissing:
      cur = whenMissing(cur.missingKey, simplify(cur.body))
    if isWrite(cur):
      while result.len > 0 and isWrite(result[^1]) and writtenKey(result[^1]) == writtenKey(cur):
        result.delete(result.high)
    result.add cur
```

Write the Nim module `functional_core.nim` (Functional core, imperative shell).

Functional core, imperative shell: decide with a pure function, act with a thin loop.

The core is a `func` from (configuration, current state, new input) to a decision: the next
state plus a list of effect descriptions, which are plain data. It never touches the world, so
every rule about when the system acts is a property of a function. The shell is the small loop
that reads an input, calls the core and performs the effects it returned; it holds no rules.
Use it whenever logic and I/O are tangled. The example is a thermostat with a dead band: it
switches only when the reading leaves the band, so the same reading twice never acts twice.

```nim
  band*: int                 ## half-width of the dead band, never negative (see `initConfig`)
type EffectKind = enum
  ekSetHeater, ekLog
type Effect = object
  case kind*: EffectKind
  of ekSetHeater:
    heater*: HeaterState
  of ekLog:
    line*: string
type Decision = object
  state*: HeaterState
  effects*: seq[Effect]
func `==`(a, b: Effect): bool
func initConfig(target, band: int): Result[Config, string]
func decide(cfg: Config; current: HeaterState; reading: int): Decision
```

```nim
## Functional core, imperative shell: decide with a pure function, act with a thin loop.
##
## The core is a `func` from (configuration, current state, new input) to a decision: the next
## state plus a list of effect descriptions, which are plain data. It never touches the world, so
## every rule about when the system acts is a property of a function. The shell is the small loop
## that reads an input, calls the core and performs the effects it returned; it holds no rules.
## Use it whenever logic and I/O are tangled. The example is a thermostat with a dead band: it
## switches only when the reading leaves the band, so the same reading twice never acts twice.

import nimcs/fp/result

type
  HeaterState* = enum
    hsOff, hsOn

  Config* = object
    ## Temperatures are in tenths of a degree.
    target*: int
    band*: int   ## half-width of the dead band, never negative (see `initConfig`)

  EffectKind* = enum
    ekSetHeater, ekLog

  Effect* = object
    ## An effect described, not performed. The shell decides how to perform it.
    case kind*: EffectKind
    of ekSetHeater:
      heater*: HeaterState
    of ekLog:
      line*: string

  Decision* = object
    state*: HeaterState
    effects*: seq[Effect]

func `==`*(a, b: Effect): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of ekSetHeater: a.heater == b.heater
  of ekLog: a.line == b.line

func initConfig*(target, band: int): Result[Config, string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Smart constructor: a negative band has no meaning.
  if band < 0: err(Config, "band must not be negative")
  else: ok(Config(target: target, band: band), string)

func decide*(cfg: Config; current: HeaterState; reading: int): Decision {.raises: [].} =
  ## Pure decision. Inside the dead band (`|reading - target| <= band`) the state is kept and no
  ## effect is emitted; outside it the heater is driven toward the target, and a change is
  ## reported as one `ekSetHeater` followed by one `ekLog`.
  let wanted =
    if reading < cfg.target - cfg.band: hsOn
    elif reading > cfg.target + cfg.band: hsOff
    else: current
  if wanted == current:
    Decision(state: current, effects: @[])
  else:
    let word = if wanted == hsOn: "on" else: "off"
    Decision(state: wanted, effects: @[
      Effect(kind: ekSetHeater, heater: wanted),
      Effect(kind: ekLog, line: "heater " & word & " at " & $reading)])
```

Idempotent command: the same command with the same key is applied once, however often it arrives.

Networks deliver at least once, so a client that did not hear back sends the command again.
Each command carries a key chosen by the client. The ledger stores, for every key it has
seen, the command and the response it produced; a repeat of the same command returns the
stored response and changes nothing, and a different command under a used key is a conflict.
`handle` is a pure function from (ledger, command) to (ledger, response), so "applying twice
equals applying once" is a property of a function, not a hope about a server. Use it for any
operation a client may retry (payments, orders, sign-ups). In production the entry list
would be a keyed table with an expiry; the list keeps the example short and ordered.

```nim
  ckDeposit, ckWithdraw

  kind*: CommandKind
  amount*: int
type ResponseKind = enum
  rkAccepted, rkInsufficientFunds, rkInvalidAmount, rkKeyConflict
type Response = object
  kind*: ResponseKind
  balance*: int
type Entry = object
  cmd*: Command
  response*: Response
type Ledger = object
  balance*: int
  entries*: seq[Entry]       ## in order of first arrival; one per key
type Handled = tuple[ledger: Ledger, response: Response]
func initLedger(): Ledger
func handle(l: Ledger; cmd: Command): Handled
```

```nim
## Idempotent command: the same command with the same key is applied once, however often it arrives.
##
## Networks deliver at least once, so a client that did not hear back sends the command again.
## Each command carries a key chosen by the client. The ledger stores, for every key it has
## seen, the command and the response it produced; a repeat of the same command returns the
## stored response and changes nothing, and a different command under a used key is a conflict.
## `handle` is a pure function from (ledger, command) to (ledger, response), so "applying twice
## equals applying once" is a property of a function, not a hope about a server. Use it for any
## operation a client may retry (payments, orders, sign-ups). In production the entry list
## would be a keyed table with an expiry; the list keeps the example short and ordered.

type
  CommandKind* = enum
    ckDeposit, ckWithdraw

  Command* = object
    key*: string
    kind*: CommandKind
    amount*: int

  ResponseKind* = enum
    rkAccepted, rkInsufficientFunds, rkInvalidAmount, rkKeyConflict

  Response* = object
    ## `balance` is the balance the command left (accepted) or found (every refusal that was
    ## stored); for a conflict it is the current balance.
    kind*: ResponseKind
    balance*: int

  Entry* = object
    cmd*: Command
    response*: Response

  Ledger* = object
    balance*: int
    entries*: seq[Entry]   ## in order of first arrival; one per key

  Handled* = tuple[ledger: Ledger, response: Response]

func initLedger*(): Ledger {.raises: [].} = Ledger(balance: 0, entries: @[])

func decideNew(l: Ledger; cmd: Command): Handled {.raises: [].} =
  ## First arrival of a key: decide, then record the outcome under the key.
  var balance = l.balance
  var kind = rkAccepted
  if cmd.amount <= 0:
    kind = rkInvalidAmount
  else:
    case cmd.kind
    of ckDeposit:
      balance += cmd.amount
    of ckWithdraw:
      if balance < cmd.amount: kind = rkInsufficientFunds
      else: balance -= cmd.amount
  let response = Response(kind: kind, balance: balance)
  var entries = l.entries
  entries.add Entry(cmd: cmd, response: response)
  (ledger: Ledger(balance: balance, entries: entries), response: response)

func handle*(l: Ledger; cmd: Command): Handled {.raises: [].} =
  ## A key seen before returns its stored response and the same ledger when the command is
  ## identical, and `rkKeyConflict` (ledger unchanged, nothing stored) when it is not. A new key
  ## is decided once; refusals are stored too, so a retry sees the same refusal even if the
  ## balance would now allow the command.
  for e in l.entries:
    if e.cmd.key == cmd.key:
      if e.cmd == cmd:
        return (ledger: l, response: e.response)
      return (ledger: l, response: Response(kind: rkKeyConflict, balance: l.balance))
  decideNew(l, cmd)
```

```nim
## Interpreter: a grammar is a data type and the interpreter is a fold over it.
##
## The OO pattern gives each grammar rule a class with an `interpret(context)` method. In Nim the
## rules are the cases of one object variant (`Expr`), and each interpretation (evaluate, print,
## simplify) is one `func` with an exhaustive `case`. Adding an interpretation never touches the
## type; variable names are validated by `variable`, so `show` is injective. Adding a rule makes every `case` fail to compile until it is handled. Use it for small
## languages (formulas, filters, rules). For a full language reach for a parser generator and keep
## this shape for the tree after parsing.
##
## Arithmetic here is checked: every value must stay within `+-Limit`, so no operation can
## overflow `int`. Division by zero, an unbound variable and a limit breach are `EvalError`s.

import std/options
import nimcs/fp/result

const Limit* = 1_000_000_000

type
  ExprKind* = enum
    ekNum, ekVar, ekNeg, ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv

  Expr* = ref object
    ## Immutable: the fields are private, so a node can only be made by the constructors below
    ## (`num`, `variable`, `neg`, `add`, `mul`, `divide`) and read through the accessors. That is
    ## what keeps variable names valid. Reading an accessor of the wrong kind (`num` of an `ekAdd`)
    ## is a precondition violation: test `kind` first, as the `case` in `eval` does.
    case kind: ExprKind
    of ekNum:
      num: int
    of ekVar:
      name: string
    of ekNeg:
      operand: Expr
    of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv:
      left, right: Expr

  Binding* = (string, int)

  EvalError* = enum
    evUnbound, evDivByZero, evLimit

  VarError* = enum
    veBadName   ## a variable name must be an identifier

func kind*(e: Expr): ExprKind {.raises: [].} = e.kind
func num*(e: Expr): int {.raises: [].} = e.num
func name*(e: Expr): string {.raises: [].} = e.name
func operand*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = e.operand
func left*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = e.left
func right*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = e.right

func num*(n: int): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekNum, num: n)
func isIdentifier(s: string): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if s.len == 0: return false
  for i, c in s:
    let letter = c in {'a' .. 'z', 'A' .. 'Z', '_'}
    if not (letter or (i > 0 and c in {'0' .. '9'})): return false
  true

func variable*(name: string): Result[Expr, VarError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Smart constructor. A name is a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits and
  ## underscores; anything else (spaces, parentheses, operators, empty) would make `show` ambiguous
  ## and is refused. Build `Expr` nodes through the constructors, not by naming `ekVar` directly.
  if isIdentifier(name): ok(Expr(kind: ekVar, name: name), VarError)
  else: err(Expr, veBadName)
func neg*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekNeg, operand: e)
func add*(a, b: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekAdd, left: a, right: b)
func mul*(a, b: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekMul, left: a, right: b)
func divide*(a, b: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekDiv, left: a, right: b)

func same*(a, b: Expr): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Structural equality.
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of ekNum: a.num == b.num
  of ekVar: a.name == b.name
  of ekNeg: same(a.operand, b.operand)
  of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv: same(a.left, b.left) and same(a.right, b.right)

func show*(e: Expr): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## One interpretation: a fully parenthesised rendering.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum: $e.num
  of ekVar: e.name
  of ekNeg: "(-" & show(e.operand) & ")"
  of ekAdd: "(" & show(e.left) & " + " & show(e.right) & ")"
  of ekMul: "(" & show(e.left) & " * " & show(e.right) & ")"
  of ekDiv: "(" & show(e.left) & " / " & show(e.right) & ")"

func size*(e: Expr): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Number of nodes.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum, ekVar: 1
  of ekNeg: 1 + size(e.operand)
  of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv: 1 + size(e.left) + size(e.right)

func checked(n: int): Result[int, EvalError] {.raises: [].} =
  if n > Limit or n < -Limit: err(int, evLimit) else: ok(n, EvalError)

func lookup(env: openArray[Binding]; name: string): Option[int] {.raises: [].} =
  for b in env:
    if b[0] == name: return some(b[1])
  none(int)

func combine(kind: ExprKind; a, b: int): Result[int, EvalError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The meaning of one binary node. Both operands are range-checked here, so `eval` and `fold`
  ## (which may hand over raw literals) agree on every input, including out-of-range literals.
  let ca = checked(a)
  if ca.isErr: return ca
  let cb = checked(b)
  if cb.isErr: return cb
  case kind
  of ekAdd: checked(a + b)
  of ekMul: checked(a * b)
  of ekDiv:
    if b == 0: err(int, evDivByZero) else: checked(a div b)
  of ekNum, ekVar, ekNeg: err(int, evLimit)   # not binary; unreachable through `eval`/`fold`

func eval*(e: Expr; env: openArray[Binding]): Result[int, EvalError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Left operand first, so the first error in reading order is the one reported.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum: checked(e.num)
  of ekVar:
    let v = lookup(env, e.name)
    if v.isNone: err(int, evUnbound) else: checked(v.get)
  of ekNeg:
    let r = eval(e.operand, env)
    if r.isErr: r else: checked(-r.value)
  of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv:
    let l = eval(e.left, env)
    if l.isErr: return l
    let r = eval(e.right, env)
    if r.isErr: return r
    combine(e.kind, l.value, r.value)

func foldBinary(kind: ExprKind; l, r: Expr;
                rebuild: proc(a, b: Expr): Expr {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Expr {.raises: [].} =
  if l.kind == ekNum and r.kind == ekNum:
    let v = combine(kind, l.num, r.num)
    if v.isOk: return num(v.value)
  rebuild(l, r)

func fold*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} =
  ## Constant folding: replaces every subtree made only of numbers that evaluates successfully.
  ## A subtree that would fail (division by zero, limit) is kept, so `eval` still reports it.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum, ekVar: e
  of ekNeg:
    let o = fold(e.operand)
    if o.kind == ekNum:
      let inRange = checked(o.num)   # -low(int) would overflow, so check before negating
      if inRange.isOk:
        let r = checked(-o.num)
        if r.isOk: return num(r.value)
    neg(o)
  of ekAdd: foldBinary(ekAdd, fold(e.left), fold(e.right), add)
  of ekMul: foldBinary(ekMul, fold(e.left), fold(e.right), mul)
  of ekDiv: foldBinary(ekDiv, fold(e.left), fold(e.right), divide)
```

Iterator: traversal is a Nim `iterator`, or a cursor that is itself a value.

The OO pattern hides a collection's structure behind an object with `hasNext`/`next`. Nim has the
pattern built in: an `iterator` is the traversal and a `for` loop is the client. Two shapes are
shown over an immutable binary search tree. `items` is an inline iterator (internal iteration:
the loop body runs inside the traversal). `Cursor` is external iteration done functionally: a
value holding the traversal's pending work, where `next` returns the element and the *next
cursor*, so a cursor can be kept, copied and resumed any number of times. External iteration is
what you need to walk two collections in lockstep (`mergeUnion`). Use `iterator` first; reach
for `Cursor` only when two traversals must advance independently.

Public API:

```nim
type Cursor = object

func next(c: Cursor): Option[(int, Cursor)]

func toSeq(t: Tree): seq[int]
func mergeUnion(a, b: Tree): seq[int]
```

```nim
## Iterator: traversal is a Nim `iterator`, or a cursor that is itself a value.
##
## The OO pattern hides a collection's structure behind an object with `hasNext`/`next`. Nim has the
## pattern built in: an `iterator` is the traversal and a `for` loop is the client. Two shapes are
## shown over an immutable binary search tree. `items` is an inline iterator (internal iteration:
## the loop body runs inside the traversal). `Cursor` is external iteration done functionally: a
## value holding the traversal's pending work, where `next` returns the element and the *next
## cursor*, so a cursor can be kept, copied and resumed any number of times. External iteration is
## what you need to walk two collections in lockstep (`mergeUnion`). Use `iterator` first; reach
## for `Cursor` only when two traversals must advance independently.

import std/options

type
  Tree* = ref Node
    ## Empty tree is `nil`. Nodes are immutable by convention.
  Node = object
    left, right: Tree
    value: int

  Cursor* = object
    ## The left spine still to visit; the top of `pending` is the next element.
    pending: seq[Tree]

func insert*(t: Tree; v: int): Tree {.raises: [].} =
  ## Returns a new tree containing `v`; `t` is unchanged and shares its untouched subtrees.
  ## A value already present is not added again (set semantics).
  if t.isNil: return Tree(value: v)
  if v < t.value: Tree(value: t.value, left: insert(t.left, v), right: t.right)
  elif v > t.value: Tree(value: t.value, left: t.left, right: insert(t.right, v))
  else: t

func fromSeq*(xs: openArray[int]): Tree {.raises: [].} =
  for x in xs: result = result.insert(x)

func pushSpine(stack: seq[Tree]; t: Tree): seq[Tree] {.raises: [].} =
  result = stack
  var cur = t
  while not cur.isNil:
    result.add cur
    cur = cur.left

func cursor*(t: Tree): Cursor {.raises: [].} =
  Cursor(pending: pushSpine(@[], t))

func next*(c: Cursor): Option[(int, Cursor)] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The next element in ascending order and the cursor after it; `none` at the end.
  if c.pending.len == 0: return none((int, Cursor))
  let node = c.pending[^1]
  let rest = c.pending[0 ..< c.pending.len - 1]
  some((node.value, Cursor(pending: pushSpine(rest, node.right))))

iterator items*(t: Tree): int =
  ## In-order (ascending) traversal. Internal iteration: use it in a `for` loop.
  var c = cursor(t)
  while true:
    let n = c.next
    if n.isNone: break
    yield n.get[0]
    c = n.get[1]

func toSeq*(t: Tree): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  for x in t.items: result.add x

func mergeUnion*(a, b: Tree): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending union of two trees, each element once, walking both with cursors in lockstep.
  var ca = cursor(a)
  var cb = cursor(b)
  while true:
    let na = ca.next
    let nb = cb.next
    if na.isNone and nb.isNone: break
    if nb.isNone or (na.isSome and na.get[0] < nb.get[0]):
      result.add na.get[0]
      ca = na.get[1]
    elif na.isNone or nb.get[0] < na.get[0]:
      result.add nb.get[0]
      cb = nb.get[1]
    else:
      result.add na.get[0]
      ca = na.get[1]
      cb = nb.get[1]
```

```nim
## Lens: a getter and a setter bundled so that a deep field of an immutable value can be read and replaced.
##
## Updating `company.ceo.address.city` in immutable data means rebuilding three levels by hand.
## A `Lens[S, A]` focuses on an `A` inside an `S`: `view` reads it, `put` returns a new `S` with
## it replaced, and `compose` chains a lens into a lens so deep access is the composition of
## shallow ones. A lens is only trustworthy if it obeys three laws (get-set, set-get, set-set),
## which are properties to test for every lens you write. Use lenses for nested records that are
## updated often; for one field one level down, plain object copy (`fp/immutable_update`) is
## simpler.

type
  Address* = object
    street*, city*: string
    zip*: int

  Person* = object
    name*: string
    age*: int
    address*: Address

  Company* = object
    name*: string
    ceo*: Person

  Lens*[S, A] = object
    getter: proc(s: S): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    setter: proc(s: S; a: A): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func lens*[S, A](getter: proc(s: S): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].};
                 setter: proc(s: S; a: A): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Lens[S, A] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Bundles a getter and a setter. Nothing checks the laws; test them.
  Lens[S, A](getter: getter, setter: setter)

func view*[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S): A {.raises: [].} = l.getter(s)

func put*[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S; a: A): S {.raises: [].} =
  ## A copy of `s` with the focus replaced; `s` is untouched.
  l.setter(s, a)

func over*[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S; f: proc(a: A): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): S {.raises: [].} =
  ## Replaces the focus by `f` of the focus.
  l.put(s, f(l.view(s)))

func compose*[S, M, A](outer: Lens[S, M]; inner: Lens[M, A]): Lens[S, A] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Focuses first through `outer`, then through `inner`.
  lens(
    proc(s: S): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = inner.view(outer.view(s)),
    proc(s: S; a: A): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = outer.put(s, inner.put(outer.view(s), a)))

# ── lenses for the example records ─────────────────────────────────────────

func companyCeo*(): Lens[Company, Person] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(c: Company): Person {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = c.ceo,
    proc(c: Company; p: Person): Company {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = Company(name: c.name, ceo: p))

func addressLens*(): Lens[Person, Address] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(p: Person): Address {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = p.address,
    proc(p: Person; a: Address): Person {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Person(name: p.name, age: p.age, address: a))

func ageLens*(): Lens[Person, int] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(p: Person): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = p.age,
    proc(p: Person; a: int): Person {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Person(name: p.name, age: a, address: p.address))

func cityLens*(): Lens[Address, string] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(a: Address): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a.city,
    proc(a: Address; c: string): Address {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Address(street: a.street, city: c, zip: a.zip))

func ceoAge*(): Lens[Company, int] {.raises: [].} =
  companyCeo().compose(ageLens())

func ceoCity*(): Lens[Company, string] {.raises: [].} =
  companyCeo().compose(addressLens()).compose(cityLens())
```

Mediator: participants never address each other; a pure routing function does.

The OO pattern puts the knowledge of "who talks to whom" into one mediator object so the
colleagues stay decoupled. In Nim the colleagues are just names in a room value, a message is
data, and the mediator is `route(room, message)`, which returns the new room and the list of
deliveries (who receives what). Nothing is sent from inside; the caller performs the deliveries,
so the whole chat logic is testable without sockets. Use it when many parties interact by rules
(chat, form-field dependencies, air-traffic hand-offs). Members are kept sorted, so delivery
order is deterministic.
