```nim
## Mediator: participants never address each other; a pure routing function does.
##
## The OO pattern puts the knowledge of "who talks to whom" into one mediator object so the
## colleagues stay decoupled. In Nim the colleagues are just names in a room value, a message is
## data, and the mediator is `route(room, message)`, which returns the new room and the list of
## deliveries (who receives what). Nothing is sent from inside; the caller performs the deliveries,
## so the whole chat logic is testable without sockets. Use it when many parties interact by rules
## (chat, form-field dependencies, air-traffic hand-offs). Members are kept sorted, so delivery
## order is deterministic.

import std/[algorithm, strutils]
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  MsgKind* = enum
    mkJoin, mkLeave, mkSay, mkWhisper

  Msg* = object
    sender*: string
    case kind*: MsgKind
    of mkJoin, mkLeave: discard
    of mkSay:
      text*: string
    of mkWhisper:
      to*: string
      secret*: string

  Delivery* = object
    to*: string
    body*: string

  Room* = object
    members: seq[string]   ## sorted, no duplicates

  RoomError* = enum
    reAlreadyMember, reNotMember, reNoSuchRecipient, reSelfWhisper

  Routed* = object
    room*: Room
    deliveries*: seq[Delivery]

  RunReport* = object
    room*: Room
    deliveries*: seq[Delivery]
    rejected*: seq[(int, RoomError)]   ## (index in the log, reason)

func `==`*(a, b: Delivery): bool {.raises: [].} = a.to == b.to and a.body == b.body
func `==`*(a, b: Room): bool {.raises: [].} = a.members == b.members
func `==`*(a, b: Routed): bool {.raises: [].} = a.room == b.room and a.deliveries == b.deliveries
func `==`*(a, b: RunReport): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.room == b.room and a.deliveries == b.deliveries and a.rejected == b.rejected
func `$`*(d: Delivery): string {.raises: [].} = d.to & ": " & d.body
func `$`*(r: Room): string {.raises: [].} = "Room(" & r.members.join(",") & ")"

func join*(name: string): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mkJoin, sender: name)
func leave*(name: string): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mkLeave, sender: name)
func say*(name, text: string): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mkSay, sender: name, text: text)
func whisper*(name, to, text: string): Msg {.raises: [].} =
  Msg(kind: mkWhisper, sender: name, to: to, secret: text)

func emptyRoom*(): Room {.raises: [].} = Room(members: @[])
func members*(r: Room): seq[string] {.raises: [].} = r.members
func has*(r: Room; name: string): bool {.raises: [].} = name in r.members

func route*(room: Room; m: Msg): Result[Routed, RoomError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The mediator. Joins and leaves are announced to everyone else; a say reaches every member but
  ## the sender; a whisper reaches exactly its recipient.
  case m.kind
  of mkJoin:
    if room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reAlreadyMember)
    let next = Room(members: (room.members & m.sender).sorted)
    var ds: seq[Delivery]
    for who in room.members: ds.add Delivery(to: who, body: m.sender & " joined")
    ok(Routed(room: next, deliveries: ds), RoomError)
  of mkLeave:
    if not room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reNotMember)
    var rest: seq[string]
    for who in room.members:
      if who != m.sender: rest.add who
    var ds: seq[Delivery]
    for who in rest: ds.add Delivery(to: who, body: m.sender & " left")
    ok(Routed(room: Room(members: rest), deliveries: ds), RoomError)
  of mkSay:
    if not room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reNotMember)
    var ds: seq[Delivery]
    for who in room.members:
      if who != m.sender: ds.add Delivery(to: who, body: m.sender & ": " & m.text)
    ok(Routed(room: room, deliveries: ds), RoomError)
  of mkWhisper:
    if not room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reNotMember)
    if m.to == m.sender: return err(Routed, reSelfWhisper)
    if not room.has(m.to): return err(Routed, reNoSuchRecipient)
    ok(Routed(room: room, deliveries: @[Delivery(to: m.to,
        body: m.sender & " (private): " & m.secret)]), RoomError)

func runLog*(room: Room; log: openArray[Msg]): RunReport {.raises: [].} =
  ## Routes a whole log. A message the room rejects delivers nothing and leaves the room as it
  ## was; its index and reason are listed in `rejected`, in log order, so nothing is lost.
  result = RunReport(room: room, deliveries: @[], rejected: @[])
  for i, m in log:
    let r = route(result.room, m)
    if r.isOk:
      result.room = r.value.room
      result.deliveries.add r.value.deliveries
    else:
      result.rejected.add (i, r.error)
```

Write the Nim module `memento.nim` (Memento).

Memento: a snapshot is just an old value.

The OO pattern exists because objects are mutable and hide their fields: to roll one back, you
need a sealed copy of its private state that only the object can open. With value semantics the
problem disappears: `let saved = settings` is the memento, later changes build *new* values and
cannot reach it. The guarantee holds for values made of value fields; a `ref` field is copied as a
pointer, so the data behind it is shared and a later change through the original shows in the
snapshot (GOF-MEMENTO-08). Keep snapshotted state free of mutable `ref`s, or rebuild the referent
when snapshotting. What is left to design is the history policy, shown here as `Timeline[T]`: the
values before the present, the present, the values that were undone, and a capacity so the past
cannot grow without bound. Use it for undo-by-snapshot of small or structurally shared values;
for large state or replication, store commands instead (see `command`).

```nim
func pastLen[T](t: Timeline[T]): int
func futureLen[T](t: Timeline[T]): int
func history[T](t: Timeline[T]): seq[T]
func record[T](t: Timeline[T]; v: T): Timeline[T]
func undo[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]]
func redo[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]]
```

```nim
## Memento: a snapshot is just an old value.
##
## The OO pattern exists because objects are mutable and hide their fields: to roll one back, you
## need a sealed copy of its private state that only the object can open. With value semantics the
## problem disappears: `let saved = settings` is the memento, later changes build *new* values and
## cannot reach it. The guarantee holds for values made of value fields; a `ref` field is copied as a
## pointer, so the data behind it is shared and a later change through the original shows in the
## snapshot (GOF-MEMENTO-08). Keep snapshotted state free of mutable `ref`s, or rebuild the referent
## when snapshotting. What is left to design is the history policy, shown here as `Timeline[T]`: the
## values before the present, the present, the values that were undone, and a capacity so the past
## cannot grow without bound. Use it for undo-by-snapshot of small or structurally shared values;
## for large state or replication, store commands instead (see `command`).

import std/options

type
  Timeline*[T] = object
    past: seq[T]      ## oldest first
    present: T
    future: seq[T]    ## the value to redo next is last
    capacity: int     ## at most this many past values are kept (>= 1)

func initTimeline*[T](start: T; capacity: int): Timeline[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `capacity` below 1 is raised to 1 so that one undo is always possible.
  Timeline[T](past: @[], present: start, future: @[], capacity: max(1, capacity))

func current*[T](t: Timeline[T]): T {.raises: [].} = t.present
func pastLen*[T](t: Timeline[T]): int {.raises: [].} = t.past.len
func futureLen*[T](t: Timeline[T]): int {.raises: [].} = t.future.len
func history*[T](t: Timeline[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Oldest first, ending with the present.
  t.past & t.present

func record*[T](t: Timeline[T]; v: T): Timeline[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Makes `v` the present. The old present becomes the newest past value, the oldest past value
  ## is dropped when the capacity is exceeded, and redo is cleared.
  var past = t.past & t.present
  if past.len > t.capacity: past = past[past.len - t.capacity .. ^1]
  Timeline[T](past: past, present: v, future: @[], capacity: t.capacity)

func undo*[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  if t.past.len == 0: return none(Timeline[T])
  some(Timeline[T](past: t.past[0 ..< t.past.len - 1], present: t.past[^1],
                   future: t.future & t.present, capacity: t.capacity))

func redo*[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  if t.future.len == 0: return none(Timeline[T])
  some(Timeline[T](past: t.past & t.present, present: t.future[^1],
                   future: t.future[0 ..< t.future.len - 1], capacity: t.capacity))
```

Write the Nim module `object_capability.nim` (Object capability).

Object capability: authority only by reference (ADR-NCK-0002).

A capability is a value that names a resource and, by existing, grants the right to use it in
specific ways. There is no ambient authority: no function here reaches a file, a global or a
clock on its own; every operation takes the capability (and the `Store` it acts on) as an
argument, so reading a signature tells you what a routine may touch. `FileCap` is sealed (a
private field and `{.requiresInit.}`), so code outside this module cannot write
`FileCap(rights: ...)` or declare an empty one; the only ways to get one are `rootCap` and the
attenuations `readOnly`, `restrict` and `narrow`, and each of them returns a capability that
permits no more than the one it came from. Delegation is passing the value.

Honest limit: Nim cannot hide `rootCap`, the one function that creates authority from nothing.
The convention is the powerbox: call it only at the program's edge (`main`), and hand narrower
capabilities inward. A review (or a text search) for `rootCap` finds every place that can
create authority. The `Store` is a plain persistent value standing for the resource; a real
program applies the same shape to a directory, a socket or a device.

Observer: an event is a value and subscribers are pure reducers folded over it.

The OO pattern keeps a mutable list of callback objects and calls each when the subject changes,
which hides ordering, mutation and re-entrancy. Here the subject does not exist as an object:
the application state `S` is a value, an event `E` is a value, and a subscriber is a named pure
function `proc(state, event): state`. Publishing is a left fold of the subscribers (in
subscription order) over the state, and the subscriber list is itself an immutable value that
`subscribe`/`unsubscribe` return a changed copy of. Because a log of events folds the same way,
replaying it reproduces the state exactly. Use it for reactive state (UI models, audit
projections). A subscriber that must do I/O belongs in the imperative shell, reading the new
state after `publish`.

```nim
##
## The OO pattern keeps a mutable list of callback objects and calls each when the subject changes,
## which hides ordering, mutation and re-entrancy. Here the subject does not exist as an object:
## the application state `S` is a value, an event `E` is a value, and a subscriber is a named pure
## function `proc(state, event): state`. Publishing is a left fold of the subscribers (in
## subscription order) over the state, and the subscriber list is itself an immutable value that

## replaying it reproduces the state exactly. Use it for reactive state (UI models, audit
## projections). A subscriber that must do I/O belongs in the imperative shell, reading the new
## state after `publish`.

type
  Reducer*[S, E] = proc(state: S; event: E): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  Subscription*[S, E] = object
    id*: string
    reduce*: Reducer[S, E]

  Bus*[S, E] = object
    subs: seq[Subscription[S, E]]   ## in subscription order

func initBus*[S, E](): Bus[S, E] {.raises: [].} =

func ids*[S, E](b: Bus[S, E]): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =

func subscribe*[S, E](b: Bus[S, E]; id: string; reduce: Reducer[S, E]): Bus[S, E] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Adds a subscriber at the end. A subscriber with the same `id` replaces the old one in place
  ## (so subscribing twice with one id is idempotent).
  result = b
  for i in 0 ..< result.subs.len:
    if result.subs[i].id == id:
      result.subs[i] = Subscription[S, E](id: id, reduce: reduce)
      return
  result.subs.add Subscription[S, E](id: id, reduce: reduce)

  ## Removes the subscriber with `id`; an unknown id changes nothing.
  result = Bus[S, E](subs: @[])
  for s in b.subs:
    if s.id != id: result.subs.add s

  ## Folds every subscriber over `state`, first subscriber first.
  result = state
  for s in b.subs: result = s.reduce(result, event)

func replay*[S, E](b: Bus[S, E]; start: S; log: openArray[E]): S {.raises: [].} =
  ## Publishes the events in order.
  result = start
  for e in log: result = b.publish(result, e)
```

Parallel change (expand, migrate, contract): change a shape without a moment when callers break.

A change to something many callers use (a column, a field, a function's argument) is done in
three steps that each leave every caller working: expand (the new shape exists next to the old
one and every writer keeps both in step), migrate (fill the new shape for data written before,
move callers one at a time) and contract (remove the old shape once nothing reads it). Here a
person's name moves from one legacy text, "Family, Given", to a `Name` with two parts. A record
holds both columns; writers through either door set both, readers fall back to translating the
other column, `backfill` fills rows that predate the change, and `contract` is a function that
refuses to drop the legacy column while any row would lose its only copy. Use it when callers
cannot all be changed in one commit or one deploy; it costs a period with two shapes, so give the
period an end.

```nim
## Pipeline: a middleware is a function from handler to handler, so a stack is function composition.
##
## A `Handler` turns a request into `Ok(response)` or `Err(error)`. A `Middleware` wraps a
## handler and returns a handler: it may refuse before calling the inner one (`requireUser`),
## change what comes back (`tagged`), or do nothing (`identity`). `andThen` composes two
## middlewares; it is associative with `identity` as unit, so any grouping of the same stack
## behaves the same and the stack is easy to test piece by piece. Handlers here are pure
## (`noSideEffect`); real logging or metrics would sit in the shell around the outermost handler.

import nimcs/fp/result

type
  Request* = object
    path*, user*, body*: string

  Response* = object
    status*: int
    body*: string

  HttpError* = object
    status*: int
    message*: string

  Handler* = proc(req: Request): Result[Response, HttpError] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  Middleware* = proc(next: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func identity*(): Middleware {.raises: [].} =
  ## Passes the inner handler through untouched.
  proc(next: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = next

func andThen*(outer, inner: Middleware): Middleware {.raises: [].} =
  ## `outer` sees the request first and the response last.
  proc(next: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = outer(inner(next))

func compose*(ms: openArray[Middleware]): Middleware {.raises: [].} =
  ## The first element is outermost; the empty list is `identity`.
  result = identity()
  for i in countdown(ms.high, 0):
    result = ms[i].andThen(result)

func requireUser*(): Middleware {.raises: [].} =
  ## Refuses a request with no user, with status 401, without calling the inner handler.
  proc(next: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(req: Request): Result[Response, HttpError] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      if req.user.len == 0:
        err(Response, HttpError(status: 401, message: "login required"))
      else:
        next(req)

func limitBody*(maxLen: int): Middleware {.raises: [].} =
  ## Refuses a body longer than `maxLen` bytes with status 413.
  proc(next: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(req: Request): Result[Response, HttpError] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      if req.body.len > maxLen:
        err(Response, HttpError(status: 413, message: "body too large"))
      else:
        next(req)

func tagged*(tag: string): Middleware {.raises: [].} =
  ## Puts `tag & ">"` in front of a successful response body; errors pass through.
  proc(next: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(req: Request): Result[Response, HttpError] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      let reply = next(req)
      if reply.isOk:
        ok(Response(status: reply.value.status, body: tag & ">" & reply.value.body), HttpError)
      else:
        reply
```

Prototype: with value semantics, copying is the default, and the pattern mostly disappears.

The OO pattern clones an existing object to avoid re-creating it and to avoid depending on its
class. In Nim an assignment already makes an independent deep copy of an `object` (including its
`seq` and `string` fields), so "clone, then change" is `let b = a` plus a `with...` func. What
remains useful is a named registry of template values (an immutable table of prototypes).
Use the registry when callers pick a template by name; otherwise just copy.

Caveat: the copy is deep only through value fields. A `ref` (or `ptr`, or a closure's captured
state) inside the object is copied as a reference, so original and copy then share the referenced
data. Keep templates free of `ref` fields, or hold such data in a value type.

```nim
## Prototype: with value semantics, copying is the default, and the pattern mostly disappears.
##
## The OO pattern clones an existing object to avoid re-creating it and to avoid depending on its
## class. In Nim an assignment already makes an independent deep copy of an `object` (including its
## `seq` and `string` fields), so "clone, then change" is `let b = a` plus a `with...` func. What
## remains useful is a named registry of template values (an immutable table of prototypes).
## Use the registry when callers pick a template by name; otherwise just copy.
##
## Caveat: the copy is deep only through value fields. A `ref` (or `ptr`, or a closure's captured
## state) inside the object is copied as a reference, so original and copy then share the referenced
## data. Keep templates free of `ref` fields, or hold such data in a value type.

import std/options

type
  Enemy* = object
    kind*: string
    hp*: int
    tags*: seq[string]

  Registry* = object
    entries: seq[(string, Enemy)]

func withHp*(e: Enemy; hp: int): Enemy {.raises: [].} =
  result = e
  result.hp = hp

func withTag*(e: Enemy; tag: string): Enemy {.raises: [].} =
  result = e
  result.tags.add(tag)

func initRegistry*(): Registry {.raises: [].} =
  Registry(entries: @[])

func register*(r: Registry; name: string; proto: Enemy): Registry {.raises: [].} =
  ## Returns a registry where `name` maps to `proto`; an earlier entry of the same name is replaced.
  result = Registry(entries: @[])
  var replaced = false
  for (n, e) in r.entries:
    if n == name:
      result.entries.add((n, proto))
      replaced = true
    else:
      result.entries.add((n, e))
  if not replaced:
    result.entries.add((name, proto))

func instantiate*(r: Registry; name: string): Option[Enemy] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A fresh, independent copy of the template, or `none`.
  for (n, e) in r.entries:
    if n == name:
      return some(e)
  none(Enemy)

func names*(r: Registry): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for (n, _) in r.entries:
    result.add(n)
```

Write the Nim module `proxy.nim` (Proxy).

Proxy as a record of procs wrapping another record of procs.

The OO pattern puts a stand-in with the same interface in front of an object to control access to
it (protection), to delay its cost (virtual) or to remember its answers (caching). In Nim the
interface is an object with a `fetch` proc field, and a fetch has three outcomes that a caller
must be able to tell apart: a value, an absent key (`ok(none)`), and a refusal (`err`).
A protection proxy (`guarded`) is a func `Source -> Source` and is fully substitutable. A cache
needs state, so `Cached` is an explicit value and `lookup` returns the updated cache: this is a
*different* interface and a `Cached` is not a `Source`. `asSource` gives a read-only view that is
a `Source` (it answers from the cache when it can, else asks the real source, and remembers
nothing). Use it when the caller must not know whether it talks to the real thing.

```nim
  misses*: int
```

```nim
## Proxy as a record of procs wrapping another record of procs.
##
## The OO pattern puts a stand-in with the same interface in front of an object to control access to
## it (protection), to delay its cost (virtual) or to remember its answers (caching). In Nim the
## interface is an object with a `fetch` proc field, and a fetch has three outcomes that a caller
## must be able to tell apart: a value, an absent key (`ok(none)`), and a refusal (`err`).
## A protection proxy (`guarded`) is a func `Source -> Source` and is fully substitutable. A cache
## needs state, so `Cached` is an explicit value and `lookup` returns the updated cache: this is a
## *different* interface and a `Cached` is not a `Source`. `asSource` gives a read-only view that is
## a `Source` (it answers from the cache when it can, else asks the real source, and remembers
## nothing). Use it when the caller must not know whether it talks to the real thing.

import std/[options, tables]
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  Refusal* = enum
    refDenied

  FetchResult* = Result[Option[string], Refusal]

  Fetch* = proc(key: string): FetchResult {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
  Allow* = proc(key: string): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  Source* = object
    fetch*: Fetch

  Cached* = object
    src: Source
    seen: Table[string, FetchResult]
    misses*: int

func guarded*(src: Source; allow: Allow): Source {.raises: [].} =
  ## Protection proxy: a denied key is answered with `err(refDenied)` and never reaches `src`.
  Source(fetch: proc(key: string): FetchResult {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    if allow(key): src.fetch(key) else: err(Option[string], refDenied))

func initCached*(src: Source): Cached {.raises: [].} =
  Cached(src: src, seen: initTable[string, FetchResult](), misses: 0)

func lookup*(c: Cached; key: string): tuple[cache: Cached, value: FetchResult] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Caching proxy: the source is asked once per key. Every answer is remembered, an absent key
  ## and a refusal included, so a source whose answers change needs a fresh `Cached`.
  if c.seen.hasKey(key):
    (c, c.seen.getOrDefault(key, ok(none(string), Refusal)))
  else:
    var next = c
    let v = c.src.fetch(key)
    next.seen[key] = v
    next.misses += 1
    (next, v)

func asSource*(c: Cached): Source {.raises: [].} =
  ## Read-only view of the cache as a `Source`; its answers equal the real source's.
  Source(fetch: proc(key: string): FetchResult {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    if c.seen.hasKey(key): c.seen.getOrDefault(key, ok(none(string), Refusal))
    else: c.src.fetch(key))
```

Write the Nim module `request_reply.nim` (Request/reply).

Request/reply: ask on top of tell, with correlation ids and a timeout that is a message
(ADR-NCK-0002).

Actors only tell. To ask, the requester sends a `Request` carrying a correlation id and its own
reply-to address, and remembers the request in a `Ledger`: a persistent map from the id to a
context the requester chose (what to do with the answer) and a deadline. The answer comes back
as a `Reply` with the same id. Waiting is not a sleep: the host schedules a timeout for the
deadline that `ask` returns and delivers it as a message, and the requester calls `onTimeout`.
Both `onReply` and `onTimeout` return the context only for the first event that settles a
request; the second one (a late reply after a timeout, a duplicate reply, an unknown id) finds
nothing pending and is dropped. So every request ends in exactly one of reply or timeout.
Time is data (`now`, `timeout` are ticks the host passes in); there is no clock here.

```nim

  id*: CorrelationId

  id*: CorrelationId
  body*: A
```

```nim
## Request/reply: ask on top of tell, with correlation ids and a timeout that is a message
## (ADR-NCK-0002).
##
## Actors only tell. To ask, the requester sends a `Request` carrying a correlation id and its own
## reply-to address, and remembers the request in a `Ledger`: a persistent map from the id to a
## context the requester chose (what to do with the answer) and a deadline. The answer comes back
## as a `Reply` with the same id. Waiting is not a sleep: the host schedules a timeout for the
## deadline that `ask` returns and delivers it as a message, and the requester calls `onTimeout`.
## Both `onReply` and `onTimeout` return the context only for the first event that settles a
## request; the second one (a late reply after a timeout, a duplicate reply, an unknown id) finds
## nothing pending and is dropped. So every request ends in exactly one of reply or timeout.
## Time is data (`now`, `timeout` are ticks the host passes in); there is no clock here.

import std/options
import nimcs/ds/hamt
import nimcs/patterns/actor

type
  CorrelationId* = distinct int
    ## Allocated by the ledger, increasing, never reused.

  Request*[Q] = object
    id*: CorrelationId
    replyTo*: Address
    body*: Q

  Reply*[A] = object
    id*: CorrelationId
    body*: A

  Entry[C] = object
    context: C
    deadline: int

  Ledger*[C] = object
    ## The requests still waiting for an answer.
    next: int
    waiting: Hamt[int, Entry[C]]

  Asked*[C, Q] = object
    ledger*: Ledger[C]
    request*: Request[Q]     ## to send to the server
    deadline*: int           ## when the host should deliver the timeout

func `==`*(a, b: CorrelationId): bool {.borrow.}
func `$`*(a: CorrelationId): string {.borrow.}

func initLedger*[C](): Ledger[C] {.raises: [].} =
  Ledger[C](next: 0, waiting: emptyHamt[int, Entry[C]]())

func pendingCount*[C](l: Ledger[C]): int {.raises: [].} = l.waiting.len

func isPending*[C](l: Ledger[C]; id: CorrelationId): bool {.raises: [].} =
  l.waiting.contains(int(id))

func addSaturating(a, b: int): int =
  if b > 0 and a > high(int) - b: high(int)
  elif b < 0 and a < low(int) - b: low(int)
  else: a + b

func ask*[Q, C](l: Ledger[C]; replyTo: Address; body: Q; context: C; now, timeout: int):
    Asked[C, Q] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Makes a request and remembers `context` until it is settled. The deadline is `now + timeout`
  ## (saturating); a timeout of 0 or less is due at once.
  let deadline = addSaturating(now, timeout)
  Asked[C, Q](
    ledger: Ledger[C](next: l.next + 1,
      waiting: l.waiting.put(l.next, Entry[C](context: context, deadline: deadline))),
    request: Request[Q](id: CorrelationId(l.next), replyTo: replyTo, body: body),
    deadline: deadline)

func replyWith*[Q, A](req: Request[Q]; body: A): Reply[A] {.raises: [].} =
  ## What the server sends to `req.replyTo`.
  Reply[A](id: req.id, body: body)

func settle[C](l: Ledger[C]; id: CorrelationId): (Ledger[C], Option[C]) =
  let e = l.waiting.get(int(id))
  if e.isNone: (l, none(C))
  else: (Ledger[C](next: l.next, waiting: l.waiting.remove(int(id))), some(e.get.context))

func onReply*[A, C](l: Ledger[C]; reply: Reply[A]): (Ledger[C], Option[C]) {.raises: [].} =
  ## `some(context)` if this reply settled a pending request; `none` (ledger unchanged) if the
  ## request already ended or never existed.
  l.settle(reply.id)

func onTimeout*[C](l: Ledger[C]; id: CorrelationId): (Ledger[C], Option[C]) {.raises: [].} =
  ## `some(context)` if the request was still pending; `none` (ledger unchanged) if a reply won.
  l.settle(id)

func dueAt*[C](l: Ledger[C]; now: int): seq[CorrelationId] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The pending requests whose deadline is `now` or earlier, in id order. For a host that polls
  ## instead of scheduling one timer per request.
  for (k, e) in l.waiting.toSortedSeq:
    if e.deadline <= now: result.add CorrelationId(k)
```

```nim
## Retry with backoff: the policy is data, `nextDelay` is a pure function, only the sleeping is effect.
##
## After the n-th failure a client waits before trying again; the wait grows geometrically up to
## a cap, and a jitter spreads out clients that failed together. Here the policy is a validated
## record and `nextDelay(failures, jitter)` is a function of it: it returns the delay in
## milliseconds, or `none` when the attempts are used up. The jitter is an argument (a per-mille
## value), derived from a seed by `jitterFor`, so the schedule is reproducible and testable
## without a clock or a random source. The loop that calls the operation and actually sleeps is
## the imperative shell and lives with the caller. Use it for any retried call to a flaky
## dependency.

import std/options
import nimcs/fp/result

const MaxCapMs* = 86_400_000  ## one day; keeps every intermediate product far below int range

type
  Permille* = range[0 .. 999]
    ## A jitter sample: the fraction of the extra delay used, in thousandths.

  RetryPolicy* = object
    baseMs: int
    capMs: int
    maxAttempts: int
    jitterPct: int

  PolicyError* = enum
    peBaseNotPositive, peCapBelowBase, peCapTooLarge, peNoAttempts, peJitterOutOfRange

func baseMs*(p: RetryPolicy): int {.raises: [].} = p.baseMs
func capMs*(p: RetryPolicy): int {.raises: [].} = p.capMs
func maxAttempts*(p: RetryPolicy): int {.raises: [].} = p.maxAttempts
func jitterPct*(p: RetryPolicy): int {.raises: [].} = p.jitterPct

func initPolicy*(baseMs, capMs, maxAttempts, jitterPct: int): Result[RetryPolicy, PolicyError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `baseMs` is the delay after the first failure; `maxAttempts` counts calls of the operation
  ## (so there are `maxAttempts - 1` waits); `jitterPct` (0..100) is how much of the step may be
  ## added on top. The first violated rule, in the order of the `PolicyError` values, is reported.
  if baseMs < 1: err(RetryPolicy, peBaseNotPositive)
  elif capMs < baseMs: err(RetryPolicy, peCapBelowBase)
  elif capMs > MaxCapMs: err(RetryPolicy, peCapTooLarge)
  elif maxAttempts < 1: err(RetryPolicy, peNoAttempts)
  elif jitterPct < 0 or jitterPct > 100: err(RetryPolicy, peJitterOutOfRange)
  else: ok(RetryPolicy(baseMs: baseMs, capMs: capMs, maxAttempts: maxAttempts, jitterPct: jitterPct), PolicyError)

func nextDelay*(p: RetryPolicy; failures: Positive; jitter: Permille): Option[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The wait after the `failures`-th failure, or `none` when `failures >= maxAttempts` (give up).
  ## The step doubles from the base up to the cap; the jitter adds at most `jitterPct` percent of
  ## the step; the sum is cut at the cap. Because the extra is at most the step, delays never
  ## decrease as `failures` grows, whatever the jitter values (PAT-RETRYBACKOFF-02).
  if failures >= p.maxAttempts:
    return none(int)
  var step = p.baseMs
  for _ in 1 ..< failures:
    if step >= p.capMs: break
    step = min(p.capMs, step * 2)
  let extra = step * p.jitterPct * jitter div 100_000
  some(min(p.capMs, step + extra))

func jitterFor*(seed: uint64; failures: Positive): Permille {.raises: [].} =
  ## A reproducible jitter sample for the given seed and failure count (a splitmix64 mix).
  var z = seed + uint64(failures) * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15'u64
  z = (z xor (z shr 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9'u64
  z = (z xor (z shr 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB'u64
  z = z xor (z shr 31)
  Permille(int(z mod 1000'u64))

func schedule*(p: RetryPolicy; seed: uint64): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Every wait the policy would produce for this seed, in order: `maxAttempts - 1` of them.
  for failures in 1 ..< p.maxAttempts:
    let d = p.nextDelay(failures, jitterFor(seed, failures))
    if d.isSome: result.add d.get

type
  RetryTrace* = object
    ## What a retry loop does for a given pattern of outcomes.
    calls*: int
    succeeded*: bool
    sleeps*: seq[int]

func simulate*(p: RetryPolicy; seed: uint64; outcomes: openArray[bool]): RetryTrace {.raises: [].} =
  ## The retry loop as a pure function. Call n succeeds when `outcomes[n - 1]` is true; a call
  ## beyond the end of `outcomes` fails. After each failure the loop waits `nextDelay` with the
  ## seed's jitter, and stops when the policy gives up. An imperative shell that really calls
  ## the operation and sleeps must make the same calls and waits.
  var attempt = 1
  while true:
    if attempt <= outcomes.len and outcomes[attempt - 1]:
      return RetryTrace(calls: attempt, succeeded: true, sleeps: result.sleeps)
    let d = p.nextDelay(attempt, jitterFor(seed, attempt))
    if d.isNone:
      return RetryTrace(calls: attempt, succeeded: false, sleeps: result.sleeps)
    result.sleeps.add d.get
    inc attempt
```

Sealer/unsealer: a matched pair of capabilities over a sealed box (ADR-NCK-0002).

position, but only the holder of the matching unsealer can read it, and whoever holds only the
sealer can seal values but not read them back. This is how a party hands out an opaque token
(a ticket, a session, a permission) that others can carry but not forge or open, and how rights
amplification works: a value's real authority sits inside a box that only the owner's
unsealer can open.

they come from a `Mint` that the program threads through the pair creations (no hidden
counter, no global). Two pairs from one mint never match, and that is the only case in which
the law "a pair's unsealer opens only its own boxes" holds: two mints started from the same
seed repeat the same brands, and their pairs then open each other's boxes. Create one mint at
the program's start and pass it on.

```nim
## Sealer/unsealer: a matched pair of capabilities over a sealed box (ADR-NCK-0002).
##
## `newPair` makes a `Sealer` and an `Unsealer` with the same brand. `seal` puts any value in a
## `Box`; `unseal` opens a box only when the unsealer's brand is the box's brand, otherwise it
## answers `seWrongBrand`. A box can be passed around, stored and compared by identity of
## position, but only the holder of the matching unsealer can read it, and whoever holds only the
## sealer can seal values but not read them back. This is how a party hands out an opaque token
## (a ticket, a session, a permission) that others can carry but not forge or open, and how rights
## amplification works: a value's real authority sits inside a box that only the owner's
## unsealer can open.
##
## All three types are sealed (private fields, `{.requiresInit.}`), so outside this module a
## brand cannot be written down, copied from a box or guessed into a value. Brands are not random:
## they come from a `Mint` that the program threads through the pair creations (no hidden
## counter, no global). Two pairs from one mint never match, and that is the only case in which
## the law "a pair's unsealer opens only its own boxes" holds: two mints started from the same
## seed repeat the same brands, and their pairs then open each other's boxes. Create one mint at
## the program's start and pass it on.

import nimcs/fp/result

type
  Mint* = object
    ## Hands out distinct brands. It is a value: `newPair` returns the next one.
    next: int

  Sealer* {.requiresInit.} = object
    brand: int

  Unsealer* {.requiresInit.} = object
    brand: int

  Box*[T] {.requiresInit.} = object
    brand: int
    content: T

  SealError* = enum
    seWrongBrand

func initMint*(seed: int): Mint {.raises: [].} = Mint(next: seed)

func newPair*(m: Mint): (Mint, Sealer, Unsealer) {.raises: [].} =
  ## A fresh pair and the mint to use for the next one.
  (Mint(next: m.next + 1), Sealer(brand: m.next), Unsealer(brand: m.next))

func seal*[T](s: Sealer; value: T): Box[T] {.raises: [].} =
  Box[T](brand: s.brand, content: value)

func unseal*[T](u: Unsealer; box: Box[T]): Result[T, SealError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The sealed value if the brands match, `err(seWrongBrand)` otherwise.
  if u.brand == box.brand: ok(box.content, SealError)
  else: err(T, seWrongBrand)
```

Seam: a place where behaviour can be changed without editing the code at that place.

Legacy code reaches for what it needs (a price list, a clock, a database) from inside, so it
cannot be run, or tested, without all of it. A seam is a point where the call can be redirected:

test supplies its own answers, and a pinned list of input and output pairs (a characterization)

becomes a seam. The old routine counted an unknown SKU as 0; the seam version says so instead

```nim
## State: the state is an object variant and a transition is a pure function.
##
## The OO pattern gives each state a class so that `insertCoin()`, `select()` ... behave
## differently per state without `if`s on a flag. In Nim the states are the cases of one object
## variant (so fields such as `credit` exist only where they mean something), and behaviour is
## `step(state, event)`: an exhaustive `case` on the phase, then on the event. An event the
## current state does not accept is a `Result` error and leaves the state as it was. The example
## is a one-product vending machine, priced in yen, which also tracks money conservation:
## everything inserted is either sold, returned, or still held. Use it for protocols, workflows
## and UI modes; when states multiply, keep one `case` per phase in its own func.

import nimcs/fp/result

const
  Price* = 120
  Coins* = [10, 50, 100, 500]

type
  Phase* = enum
    pIdle, pCredit, pReturning

  Machine* = object
    stock*: int
    inserted*: int    ## total money ever accepted
    sold*: int        ## items sold
    returned*: int    ## money handed back and collected
    case phase*: Phase
    of pIdle: discard
    of pCredit:
      credit*: int
    of pReturning:
      change*: int    ## money waiting in the tray (change or refund)

  EventKind* = enum
    evCoin, evSelect, evRefund, evCollect, evRestock

  Event* = object
    case kind*: EventKind
    of evCoin: value*: int
    of evRestock: count*: int
    of evSelect, evRefund, evCollect: discard

  VendError* = enum
    veBadCoin, veSoldOut, veNoCredit, veInsufficient, veBusyReturning, veNothingToCollect,
    veNotIdle, veBadCount

  RunReport* = object
    machine*: Machine
    rejected*: seq[(int, VendError)]   ## (index in the event list, reason)

func coin*(v: int): Event {.raises: [].} = Event(kind: evCoin, value: v)
func select*(): Event {.raises: [].} = Event(kind: evSelect)
func refund*(): Event {.raises: [].} = Event(kind: evRefund)
func collect*(): Event {.raises: [].} = Event(kind: evCollect)
func restock*(n: int): Event {.raises: [].} = Event(kind: evRestock, count: n)

func `==`*(a, b: Machine): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.phase != b.phase: return false
  if a.stock != b.stock or a.inserted != b.inserted or a.sold != b.sold or
      a.returned != b.returned: return false
  case a.phase
  of pIdle: true
  of pCredit: a.credit == b.credit
  of pReturning: a.change == b.change

func newMachine*(stock: int): Machine {.raises: [].} =
  Machine(phase: pIdle, stock: max(0, stock), inserted: 0, sold: 0, returned: 0)

func held*(m: Machine): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Money the machine holds on behalf of the customer.
  case m.phase
  of pIdle: 0
  of pCredit: m.credit
  of pReturning: m.change

func invariantHolds*(m: Machine): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Money conservation, no negative counts.
  m.stock >= 0 and m.held >= 0 and m.sold >= 0 and m.returned >= 0 and
    m.inserted == m.sold * Price + m.returned + m.held

func accepted(v: int): bool {.raises: [].} =
  for c in Coins:
    if c == v: return true

func withPhaseCredit(m: Machine; credit: int): Machine {.raises: [].} =
  Machine(phase: pCredit, credit: credit, stock: m.stock, inserted: m.inserted,
          sold: m.sold, returned: m.returned)

func withPhaseReturning(m: Machine; change: int): Machine {.raises: [].} =
  Machine(phase: pReturning, change: change, stock: m.stock, inserted: m.inserted,
          sold: m.sold, returned: m.returned)

func withPhaseIdle(m: Machine): Machine {.raises: [].} =
  Machine(phase: pIdle, stock: m.stock, inserted: m.inserted, sold: m.sold, returned: m.returned)

func step*(m: Machine; e: Event): Result[Machine, VendError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The transition table. Every (phase, event) pair is decided here, none by default.
  case m.phase
  of pIdle:
    case e.kind
    of evCoin:
      if not accepted(e.value): return err(Machine, veBadCoin)
      if m.stock == 0: return err(Machine, veSoldOut)
      var n = m.withPhaseCredit(e.value)
      n.inserted += e.value
      ok(n, VendError)
    of evSelect, evRefund: err(Machine, veNoCredit)
    of evCollect: err(Machine, veNothingToCollect)
    of evRestock:
      if e.count < 1: return err(Machine, veBadCount)
      var n = m
      n.stock += e.count
      ok(n, VendError)
  of pCredit:
    case e.kind
    of evCoin:
      if not accepted(e.value): return err(Machine, veBadCoin)
      var n = m.withPhaseCredit(m.credit + e.value)
      n.inserted += e.value
      ok(n, VendError)
    of evSelect:
      if m.credit < Price: return err(Machine, veInsufficient)
      var n = m.withPhaseReturning(m.credit - Price)
      dec n.stock
      inc n.sold
      ok(n, VendError)
    of evRefund: ok(m.withPhaseReturning(m.credit), VendError)
    of evCollect: err(Machine, veNothingToCollect)
    of evRestock: err(Machine, veNotIdle)
  of pReturning:
    case e.kind
    of evCollect:
      var n = m.withPhaseIdle()
      n.returned += m.change
      ok(n, VendError)
    of evCoin, evSelect, evRefund: err(Machine, veBusyReturning)
    of evRestock: err(Machine, veNotIdle)

func run*(m: Machine; events: openArray[Event]): RunReport {.raises: [].} =
  ## Feeds the events in order. A rejected event leaves the machine unchanged and is listed.
  result = RunReport(machine: m, rejected: @[])
  for i, e in events:
    let r = step(result.machine, e)
    if r.isOk: result.machine = r.value
    else: result.rejected.add (i, r.error)
```

State machine: the transition table is data, `step` is the only function that reads it.

A finite state machine is a set of states, a set of inputs and a table of allowed
(state, input) -> state rows. Keeping the table as a constant list, rather than nested `if`s
spread over the code, lets the same data answer other questions: which states are reachable,
which are terminal, whether any pair has two rows. `step` returns a `Result`, so a forbidden
input is a value naming the pair, never an exception. The example is an order lifecycle.

Public API:
```nim
type OrderState = enum
  osCreated, osPaid, osShipped, osDelivered, osCancelled
type Input = enum
  inPay, inShip, inDeliver, inCancel
type Transition = object
  fromState*: OrderState
  input*: Input
  toState*: OrderState
type TransitionError = object
  state*: OrderState
  input*: Input
const transitions: seq[Transition] = [(fromState: osCreated, input: inPay, toState: osPaid), (fromState: osCreated, input: inCancel, toState: osCancelled), (fromState: osPaid, input: inShip, toState: osShipped), (fromState: osPaid, input: inCancel, toState: osCancelled), (fromState: osShipped, input: inDeliver, toState: osDelivered)]
```

```nim
## State machine: the transition table is data, `step` is the only function that reads it.
##
## A finite state machine is a set of states, a set of inputs and a table of allowed
## (state, input) -> state rows. Keeping the table as a constant list, rather than nested `if`s
## spread over the code, lets the same data answer other questions: which states are reachable,
## which are terminal, whether any pair has two rows. `step` returns a `Result`, so a forbidden
## input is a value naming the pair, never an exception. The example is an order lifecycle.

import nimcs/fp/result

type
  OrderState* = enum
    osCreated, osPaid, osShipped, osDelivered, osCancelled

  Input* = enum
    inPay, inShip, inDeliver, inCancel

  Transition* = object
    fromState*: OrderState
    input*: Input
    toState*: OrderState

  TransitionError* = object
    ## The pair the table has no row for.
    state*: OrderState
    input*: Input

const transitions*: seq[Transition] = @[
  Transition(fromState: osCreated, input: inPay, toState: osPaid),
  Transition(fromState: osCreated, input: inCancel, toState: osCancelled),
  Transition(fromState: osPaid, input: inShip, toState: osShipped),
  Transition(fromState: osPaid, input: inCancel, toState: osCancelled),
  Transition(fromState: osShipped, input: inDeliver, toState: osDelivered)]

func step*(state: OrderState; input: Input): Result[OrderState, TransitionError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The one place the table is read. An absent row is an error that names the pair.
  for t in transitions:
    if t.fromState == state and t.input == input:
      return ok(t.toState, TransitionError)
  err(OrderState, TransitionError(state: state, input: input))

func run*(start: OrderState; inputs: openArray[Input]): Result[OrderState, TransitionError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Folds `step` over the inputs and stops at the first invalid one.
  var current = start
  for i in inputs:
    let next = current.step(i)
    if next.isErr: return next
    current = next.value
  ok(current, TransitionError)

func allowedInputs*(state: OrderState): seq[Input] {.raises: [].} =
  for t in transitions:
    if t.fromState == state: result.add t.input

func isTerminal*(state: OrderState): bool {.raises: [].} =
  state.allowedInputs.len == 0

func reachable*(start: OrderState): seq[OrderState] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Every state some input sequence can lead to from `start` (including `start`), in the
  ## order of the enum. Computed from the table by repeated expansion.
  var seen: set[OrderState] = {start}
  var grew = true
  while grew:
    grew = false
    for t in transitions:
      if t.fromState in seen and t.toState notin seen:
        seen.incl t.toState
        grew = true
  for s in OrderState:
    if s in seen: result.add s

func isDeterministic*(): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## True when no (state, input) pair has two rows.
  for i in 0 ..< transitions.len:
    for j in i + 1 ..< transitions.len:
      if transitions[i].fromState == transitions[j].fromState and
          transitions[i].input == transitions[j].input:
        return false
  true
```

```nim
## Strangler fig: replace a system one route at a time while the old one keeps answering.
##
## A rewrite that must be switched on in one step cannot be tried, undone or finished early. The
## strangler fig grows around the old system instead: a front door holds a table from request
## prefixes to the system that answers them, everything the table does not name still goes to the
## old system, and each step moves one prefix to the new one. The table is a value, so moving a
## prefix, moving it back, and asking whether the old system can be switched off are functions
## with laws. The observable answer changes only when the two systems disagree on a request, and
## then only for requests that follow the moved prefix. Use it when users cannot wait for a
## rewrite to be whole; it needs one front door that sees every request, and it does not by
## itself make the two systems agree (that is for tests that run both on the same requests).

import std/strutils
import nimcs/fp/result
export result

type
  Target* = enum
    tgLegacy, tgModern

  TableError* = enum
    teEmptyPrefix

  Route* = tuple[prefix: string, target: Target]

  Table* = object
    entries*: seq[Route]   ## one entry per prefix, in the order the prefixes were first named
    fallback*: Target      ## where a request goes when no prefix matches

  System* = proc(request: string): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func initTable*(): Table {.raises: [].} =
  ## Everything goes to the old system until a prefix is moved.
  Table(entries: @[], fallback: tgLegacy)

func withRoute*(t: Table; prefix: string; target: Target): Result[Table, TableError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Names a prefix; naming it again replaces its target, so the call is idempotent.
  if prefix.len == 0:
    return err(Table, teEmptyPrefix)
  var entries = t.entries
  var found = false
  for e in entries.mitems:
    if e.prefix == prefix:
      e.target = target
      found = true
  if not found:
    entries.add (prefix: prefix, target: target)
  ok(Table(entries: entries, fallback: t.fallback), TableError)

func strangle*(t: Table; prefix: string): Result[Table, TableError] {.raises: [].} =
  withRoute(t, prefix, tgModern)

func retreat*(t: Table; prefix: string): Result[Table, TableError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The way back from `strangle`: the prefix names the old system again.
  withRoute(t, prefix, tgLegacy)

func withFallback*(t: Table; target: Target): Table {.raises: [].} =
  Table(entries: t.entries, fallback: target)

func route*(t: Table; request: string): Target {.raises: [].} =
  ## The longest named prefix of the request decides; the fallback when none is a prefix.
  var best = -1
  result = t.fallback
  for e in t.entries:
    if e.prefix.len > best and request.startsWith(e.prefix):
      best = e.prefix.len
      result = e.target

func serve*(t: Table; legacy, modern: System; request: string): string {.raises: [].} =
  case t.route(request)
  of tgLegacy: legacy(request)
  of tgModern: modern(request)

func isRetired*(t: Table): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## True when no request can reach the old system, so it can be switched off.
  if t.fallback != tgModern:
    return false
  for e in t.entries:
    if e.target != tgModern:
      return false
  true
```

```nim
## Supervisor: let it crash, and decide what to restart as a pure function (ADR-NCK-0002).
##
## A worker does not defend against every failure; when it dies, its supervisor decides. The
## decision is `onExit(policy, history, child, reason, now): Decision`: a value computed from a
## sealed `Policy` (strategy, children in start order, restart intensity), the `History` of earlier
## restart times, the child that exited and why. Time is data: `now` is a tick number the host
## passes in, so the module has no clock and the decision replays exactly. The decision is one of
## ignore (the exit needs no restart), restart these children (the host stops them in reverse
## start order, then starts them in start order), or escalate (more than `maxRestarts` restarts
## within `window` ticks: the supervisor gives up, stops every child and fails its own parent).
##
## Strategies: one_for_one restarts only the child that exited; one_for_all restarts every child;
## rest_for_one restarts the child and the children started after it. A temporary child is never
## restarted, and so is never brought back as a sibling either. A restart is allowed when the
## number of restarts within the last `window` ticks, counting this one, is at most `maxRestarts`.

import std/algorithm
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  Strategy* = enum
    stOneForOne, stOneForAll, stRestForOne

  RestartKind* = enum
    rkPermanent   ## always restarted
    rkTransient   ## restarted after a crash, not after a normal exit
    rkTemporary   ## never restarted

  ExitReason* = enum
    erNormal, erCrash

  ChildSpec* = object
    id*: string
    restart*: RestartKind

  Policy* {.requiresInit.} = object
    ## Sealed: only `initPolicy` builds one, so the numbers and the children are always valid.
    strategy: Strategy
    children: seq[ChildSpec]
    maxRestarts: int
    window: int

  PolicyError* = enum
    pbNegativeIntensity, pbBadWindow, pbEmptyId, pbDuplicateChild

  ExitError* = enum
    ueUnknownChild

  History* = object
    ## The ticks of the restarts still remembered, ascending.
    ticks*: seq[int]

  DecisionKind* = enum
    dkIgnore, dkRestart, dkEscalate

  Decision* = object
    kind*: DecisionKind
    targets*: seq[string]   ## to restart (start order), or every child when escalating
    history*: History       ## the history to pass to the next `onExit`

func noHistory*(): History {.raises: [].} = History(ticks: @[])

func `==`*(a, b: History): bool {.raises: [].} = a.ticks == b.ticks

func `==`*(a, b: Decision): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.kind == b.kind and a.targets == b.targets and a.history == b.history

func record*(h: History; tick: int): History {.raises: [].} =
  ## Adds a restart time, keeping the ticks ascending.
  result = h
  result.ticks.add tick
  result.ticks.sort()

func initPolicy*(strategy: Strategy; children: seq[ChildSpec]; maxRestarts, window: int):
    Result[Policy, PolicyError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `maxRestarts` is 0 or more, `window` at least 1 tick; ids are non-empty and unique.
  if maxRestarts < 0: return err(Policy, pbNegativeIntensity)
  if window < 1: return err(Policy, pbBadWindow)
  for i, c in children:
    if c.id.len == 0: return err(Policy, pbEmptyId)
    for j in 0 ..< i:
      if children[j].id == c.id: return err(Policy, pbDuplicateChild)
  ok(Policy(strategy: strategy, children: children, maxRestarts: maxRestarts, window: window),
    PolicyError)

func childIds*(p: Policy): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for c in p.children: result.add c.id

func within(now, t, window: int): bool =
  ## Is the restart at `t` inside the last `window` ticks before `now`? The difference is taken
  ## in unsigned arithmetic so extreme ticks cannot overflow; a tick after `now` counts as inside.
  if t >= now: true
  else: uint64(now) - uint64(t) < uint64(window)

func onExit*(p: Policy; history: History; child: string; reason: ExitReason; now: int):
    Result[Decision, ExitError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## What to do when `child` exits with `reason` at tick `now`.
  var at = -1
  for i, c in p.children:
    if c.id == child: at = i
  if at < 0: return err(Decision, ueUnknownChild)
  let spec = p.children[at]
  let wanted = case spec.restart
    of rkPermanent: true
    of rkTransient: reason == erCrash
    of rkTemporary: false
  if not wanted:
    return ok(Decision(kind: dkIgnore, targets: @[], history: history), ExitError)
  var recent = noHistory()
  for t in history.ticks:
    if within(now, t, p.window): recent.ticks.add t
  if recent.ticks.len + 1 > p.maxRestarts:
    return ok(Decision(kind: dkEscalate, targets: p.childIds, history: recent), ExitError)
  var targets: seq[string]
  case p.strategy
  of stOneForOne:
    targets.add child
  of stOneForAll:
    for i, c in p.children:
      if i == at or c.restart != rkTemporary: targets.add c.id
  of stRestForOne:
    for i in at ..< p.children.len:
      if i == at or p.children[i].restart != rkTemporary: targets.add p.children[i].id
  ok(Decision(kind: dkRestart, targets: targets, history: recent.record(now)), ExitError)
```

```nim
## Template Method: the skeleton is a higher-order function and the steps are its arguments.
##
## The OO pattern fixes an algorithm's order in a base-class method and lets subclasses override
## individual steps. Nim needs no base class: the skeleton is a `func` that takes the varying
## steps as values, and a "subclass" is a `ReportSteps` value in which some fields differ from
## `defaultSteps`. The skeleton's order (header, filtered rows, footer) cannot be broken by a
## variant because variants never get to write the skeleton. Use it when several variants share
## a fixed sequence of steps. Here: a line-oriented text report, rendered as a plain list or as
## CSV with the same skeleton.

import std/strutils

type
  ReportSteps*[T] = object
    ## The varying parts. Each step is pure.
    header*: proc(shown: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    keep*: proc(item: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    row*: proc(item: T; index: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    footer*: proc(shown: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func defaultSteps*[T](): ReportSteps[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Header "Report (n items)", every item kept, row "<index>. <item>", footer "end".
  ## Rows use `$` on the item.
  ReportSteps[T](
    header: proc(shown: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = "Report (" & $shown & " items)",
    keep: proc(item: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = true,
    row: proc(item: T; index: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = $(index + 1) & ". " & $item,
    footer: proc(shown: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = "end")

func render*[T](items: openArray[T]; steps: ReportSteps[T]): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The template method. Fixed order: header, then one row per kept item, then footer, one per
  ## line. `shown` passed to header and footer is the number of kept items. Indices count kept items
  ## from 0.
  var kept: seq[T]
  for it in items:
    if steps.keep(it): kept.add it
  var lines = @[steps.header(kept.len)]
  for i, it in kept: lines.add steps.row(it, i)
  lines.add steps.footer(kept.len)
  lines.join("\n")

func withFooter*[T](s: ReportSteps[T]; footer: proc(shown: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): ReportSteps[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A variant: same steps, different footer.
  result = s
  result.footer = footer

func withKeep*[T](s: ReportSteps[T]; keep: proc(item: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): ReportSteps[T] {.raises: [].} =
  result = s
  result.keep = keep

func withRow*[T](s: ReportSteps[T]; row: proc(item: T; index: int): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): ReportSteps[T] {.raises: [].} =
  result = s
  result.row = row

func csvField*(s: string): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## RFC 4180 quoting: a field containing a comma, a double quote, CR or LF is wrapped in double
  ## quotes and its quotes are doubled; any other field is written as is.
  var needs = false
  for c in s:
    if c in {',', '"', '\r', '\n'}: needs = true
  if not needs: return s
  result = "\""
  for c in s:
    if c == '"': result.add "\"\""
    else: result.add c
  result.add '"'
```

likes (including one where only the wall clock jumped), and the same inputs give the same
answer. A time that has not happened yet is `none`, never 0: a 0 wall time shows as 1970, and

```nim
## Time as input: two clocks kept apart by type, read once at the edge, and no zero time.
##
## A program asks the time for two different reasons. To record or show a moment (a file's
## mtime, a log line, the name of a backup) it needs the wall clock, which can jump when NTP or a
## person sets it. To wait (a quiet period, a retry delay, a deadline) it needs the monotonic
## clock, which never jumps and means nothing outside the process. Here they are distinct types:
## `WallNs` and `MonoNs`, and `Span` for a length of time. Only two `MonoNs` subtract to a `Span`,
## and only a `Span` is added to a `MonoNs`, so a wait measured on the wall clock does not compile.
##
## The edge reads both clocks once, as one `Now`, and passes it in. Everything that decides is a
## `func` of that value: the compiler refuses a clock read inside it, a test builds any `Now` it
## likes (including one where only the wall clock jumped), and the same inputs give the same
## answer. A time that has not happened yet is `none`, never 0: a 0 wall time shows as 1970, and
## a 0 monotonic time is the moment the machine booted, not "long ago".
##
## The example decides when to send local changes: once the last change is `quiet` old, and not
## before the wait after a failed send (`retryAfter`) is over.

import std/[options, times, monotimes]
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  WallNs* = distinct int64
    ## Wall clock: nanoseconds since the Unix epoch. To record and show; may jump.
  MonoNs* = distinct int64
    ## Monotonic clock: nanoseconds from an origin of the process's choosing. To wait; never jumps.
  Span* = distinct int64
    ## A length of time in nanoseconds: the difference of two `MonoNs`.

  Now* = object
    ## Both clocks read at one moment, at the edge.
    wall*: WallNs
    mono*: MonoNs

  SendPolicy* {.requiresInit.} = object
    ## Sealed: only `initSendPolicy` builds one, so both spans are positive.
    quiet: Span
    retryAfter: Span

  PolicyError* = enum
    peQuietNotPositive, peRetryNotPositive

  Sender* = object
    ## What the decision remembers, as plain data.
    pending*: bool                ## local changes not yet sent
    lastChange*: Option[MonoNs]   ## none: no change since the sender began
    retryAt*: Option[MonoNs]      ## the end of the wait after a failure; none: no wait

  Action* = enum
    acWait, acSend

  SendOutcome* = enum
    soSucceeded, soFailed

func `==`*(a, b: WallNs): bool {.borrow.}
func `<`*(a, b: WallNs): bool {.borrow.}
func `<=`*(a, b: WallNs): bool {.borrow.}
func `==`*(a, b: MonoNs): bool {.borrow.}
func `<`*(a, b: MonoNs): bool {.borrow.}
func `<=`*(a, b: MonoNs): bool {.borrow.}
func `==`*(a, b: Span): bool {.borrow.}
func `<`*(a, b: Span): bool {.borrow.}
func `<=`*(a, b: Span): bool {.borrow.}

func `-`*(later, earlier: MonoNs): Span {.raises: [].} =
  ## How long passed between two readings of the monotonic clock.
  Span(int64(later) - int64(earlier))

func `+`*(t: MonoNs; d: Span): MonoNs {.raises: [].} =
  ## The monotonic time `d` after `t`.
  MonoNs(int64(t) + int64(d))

func millis*(n: int64): Span {.raises: [].} = Span(n * 1_000_000)

func seconds*(n: int64): Span {.raises: [].} = Span(n * 1_000_000_000)

func after*(n: Now; d: Span): Now {.raises: [].} =
  ## A test's clock moved on by `d`: both clocks advance together.
  Now(wall: WallNs(int64(n.wall) + int64(d)), mono: n.mono + d)

func wallJumped*(n: Now; byNs: int64): Now {.raises: [].} =
  ## A test's clock where only the wall clock was set (NTP, by hand); the monotonic one did not move.
  Now(wall: WallNs(int64(n.wall) + byNs), mono: n.mono)

func initSendPolicy*(quiet, retryAfter: Span): Result[SendPolicy, PolicyError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Both spans must be positive.
  if int64(quiet) <= 0: return err(SendPolicy, peQuietNotPositive)
  if int64(retryAfter) <= 0: return err(SendPolicy, peRetryNotPositive)
  ok(SendPolicy(quiet: quiet, retryAfter: retryAfter), PolicyError)

func idle*(): Sender {.raises: [].} =
  ## A sender with nothing to send and no wait.
  Sender(pending: false, lastChange: none(MonoNs), retryAt: none(MonoNs))

func changed*(s: Sender; now: Now): Sender {.raises: [].} =
  ## A local change was made at `now`.
  result = s
  result.pending = true
  result.lastChange = some(now.mono)

func decide*(p: SendPolicy; s: Sender; now: Now): Action {.raises: [].} =
  ## Send when there is something to send, the last change is `quiet` old and no wait after a
  ## failure is running. Only `now.mono` is read: a jump of the wall clock changes nothing.
  if not s.pending: return acWait
  if s.retryAt.isSome and now.mono < s.retryAt.get: return acWait
  if s.lastChange.isSome and now.mono - s.lastChange.get < p.quiet: return acWait
  acSend

func sent*(p: SendPolicy; s: Sender; now: Now; outcome: SendOutcome): Sender {.raises: [].} =
  ## The send decided at `now` ended. Success clears what was pending, except a change made after
  ## `now` (it was not in the send); a failure keeps everything and waits `retryAfter`.
  result = s
  if outcome == soSucceeded:
    result.pending = s.lastChange.isSome and now.mono < s.lastChange.get
    result.retryAt = none(MonoNs)
  else:
    result.retryAt = some(now.mono + p.retryAfter)

func stamp*(now: Now): WallNs {.raises: [].} =
  ## The time to record for what was sent at `now`: the wall clock of the same reading.
  now.wall

proc sample*(): Now {.raises: [].} =
  ## The edge: reads both clocks, once, at one moment. The only routine here that is not a
  ## `func`; the shell calls it and hands the value to everything above.
  let w = getTime()
  Now(wall: WallNs(w.toUnix * 1_000_000_000 + int64(w.nanosecond)), mono: MonoNs(getMonoTime().ticks))
```

Visitor: an object variant plus one exhaustive `case` per operation.

The OO pattern simulates "add an operation to a class hierarchy without editing it" with

`ShapeFold[R]` is the same traversal packaged as a first-class value: a record with one proc per

shape set: a new `ShapeKind` still means changing `Shape`, `accept` and every `ShapeFold` value.

procs instead of a shared variant (see the details page). Prefer the plain `case`.

```nim
## Visitor: an object variant plus one exhaustive `case` per operation.
##
## The OO pattern simulates "add an operation to a class hierarchy without editing it" with
## double dispatch (`accept(visitor)` calling `visitCircle`, ...). A closed set of shapes is
## already an object variant here, and each operation is a `func` with a `case` over it: adding an
## operation touches no existing code, adding a shape makes every `case` fail to compile until
## handled. That is the closed-world side of the expression problem.
##
## `ShapeFold[R]` is the same traversal packaged as a first-class value: a record with one proc per
## shape kind, applied bottom-up by `accept` (a catamorphism). It lets a caller build, store, pass
## or choose an operation at run time without writing the recursion, but it does not open the
## shape set: a new `ShapeKind` still means changing `Shape`, `accept` and every `ShapeFold` value.
## If shapes themselves must be open (added by other modules), give each shape value its own
## procs instead of a shared variant (see the details page). Prefer the plain `case`.
## Coordinates are integers, so every law is exact.

import std/options

type
  ShapeKind* = enum
    skRect, skCircle, skGroup

  Shape* = object
    case kind*: ShapeKind
    of skRect:
      x*, y*, w*, h*: int     ## top-left corner and size, w and h >= 0
    of skCircle:
      cx*, cy*, r*: int       ## centre and radius, r >= 0
    of skGroup:
      children*: seq[Shape]

  Bounds* = object
    x0*, y0*, x1*, y1*: int   ## inclusive-exclusive box: x0 <= x1, y0 <= y1

  ShapeFold*[R] = object
    ## A fold as a value: one proc per case; `group` receives the already folded children.
    rect*: proc(x, y, w, h: int): R {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    circle*: proc(cx, cy, r: int): R {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    group*: proc(children: seq[R]): R {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func `==`*(a, b: Bounds): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.x0 == b.x0 and a.y0 == b.y0 and a.x1 == b.x1 and a.y1 == b.y1

func `$`*(b: Bounds): string {.raises: [].} =
  "[" & $b.x0 & "," & $b.y0 & " .. " & $b.x1 & "," & $b.y1 & ")"

func rect*(x, y, w, h: int): Shape {.raises: [].} =
  ## Negative sizes are treated as zero.
  Shape(kind: skRect, x: x, y: y, w: max(0, w), h: max(0, h))

func circle*(cx, cy, r: int): Shape {.raises: [].} =
  Shape(kind: skCircle, cx: cx, cy: cy, r: max(0, r))

func group*(children: seq[Shape]): Shape {.raises: [].} =
  Shape(kind: skGroup, children: children)

func `==`*(a, b: Shape): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of skRect: a.x == b.x and a.y == b.y and a.w == b.w and a.h == b.h
  of skCircle: a.cx == b.cx and a.cy == b.cy and a.r == b.r
  of skGroup:
    if a.children.len != b.children.len: return false
    for i in 0 ..< a.children.len:
      if not (a.children[i] == b.children[i]): return false
    true

func leafCount*(s: Shape): int {.raises: [].} =
  case s.kind
  of skRect, skCircle: result = 1
  of skGroup:
    for c in s.children: result += leafCount(c)

func union(a, b: Bounds): Bounds {.raises: [].} =
  Bounds(x0: min(a.x0, b.x0), y0: min(a.y0, b.y0), x1: max(a.x1, b.x1), y1: max(a.y1, b.y1))

func bounds*(s: Shape): Option[Bounds] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Smallest box containing the shape; `none` for a group with no leaves.
  case s.kind
  of skRect: result = some(Bounds(x0: s.x, y0: s.y, x1: s.x + s.w, y1: s.y + s.h))
  of skCircle: result = some(Bounds(x0: s.cx - s.r, y0: s.cy - s.r, x1: s.cx + s.r, y1: s.cy + s.r))
  of skGroup:
    result = none(Bounds)
    for c in s.children:
      let b = bounds(c)
      if b.isSome:
        result = if result.isSome: some(union(result.get, b.get)) else: b

func footprint*(s: Shape): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Area of the bounding box (0 for a group with no leaves).
  let b = bounds(s)
  if b.isNone: 0 else: (b.get.x1 - b.get.x0) * (b.get.y1 - b.get.y0)

func translate*(s: Shape; dx, dy: int): Shape {.raises: [].} =
  ## A visitor that returns a new shape of the same form.
  case s.kind
  of skRect: Shape(kind: skRect, x: s.x + dx, y: s.y + dy, w: s.w, h: s.h)
  of skCircle: Shape(kind: skCircle, cx: s.cx + dx, cy: s.cy + dy, r: s.r)
  of skGroup:
    var moved: seq[Shape]
    for c in s.children: moved.add translate(c, dx, dy)
    Shape(kind: skGroup, children: moved)

func render*(s: Shape): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## A textual rendering, one tag per leaf.
  case s.kind
  of skRect: result = "<rect " & $s.x & " " & $s.y & " " & $s.w & " " & $s.h & "/>"
  of skCircle: result = "<circle " & $s.cx & " " & $s.cy & " " & $s.r & "/>"
  of skGroup:
    result = "<g>"
    for c in s.children: result.add render(c)
    result.add "</g>"

func accept*[R](s: Shape; v: ShapeFold[R]): R {.raises: [].} =
  ## Applies a record-of-procs visitor, bottom-up.
  case s.kind
  of skRect: v.rect(s.x, s.y, s.w, s.h)
  of skCircle: v.circle(s.cx, s.cy, s.r)
  of skGroup:
    var results: seq[R]
    for c in s.children: results.add accept(c, v)
    v.group(results)
```
